utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to welcome all and everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecution versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution as well as all the attorneys, the Defence counsel and the accused, and all staff members in the courtroom. I would like to greet all the attorneys, Mr. Kovacic [as interpreted], who is in the room, and I would like the person who is appearing on behalf of Mr. Coric to introduce herself. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] My name is Dijana Tomasegovic Tomic, attorney-at-law from Zagreb, and I appear for Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the Bench, we would like to welcome you in this institution. We shall proceed with the examination-in-chief, and I shall now give the floor to Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We will continue on through a number of documents, sir, and if I could ask you to look, with the registry's assistance, if you could look next at Exhibit P 00060. Very well. If you can see that document, sir. Can you look at that and confirm that that is the -- a record of the meeting of the -- of a joint meeting of the Presidency of the HDZ BiH and the HDZ BiH Crisis Staff on the 8th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your particular attention to paragraph 4, under "Conclusions." "Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall continue to advocate an independent and indivisible Bosnia and Herzegovina if that is possible," et cetera. I won't read the -- everyone can read that, I believe. Sir, did you understand that to continue -- to be the official policy of the HDZ party in Bosnia as of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the lead when these conclusions were drawn up, and it was in fact the official policy of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next paragraph immediately under that, still a continuation of part 4, makes reference again to the Commission for Cantonisation. Can you tell us anything more about what the Commission for Cantonisation was doing during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, the proposal for cantonisation was legitimate because it referred to a new administrative division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Whenever cantonisation was mentioned, reference was not being made to toppling the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina within its borders. The problem, as always with the Serbs -- was with the Serbs, as always. They were the first to put forward the idea of a new administrative division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the problem was that their pretensions were enormous and unrealistic. They wanted to control the cantonisation or, rather, they wanted to control a large part of the territories, especially those in which the Serbs were not predominant, and there the problems arose. For this reason, each one of the negotiators, both the Croatian and the Muslim side, conditionally speaking, had their own commissions working on preparing such an administrative solution which would advance the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These commissions for cantonisation were composed of eminent men, very few political officials, so one might say there were more experts in them, but their work was never completed. At least as far as we were concerned. However, the results of their work would be used later on at the Geneva negotiations, and they were to become the basis of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You said in your answer just now on page 3, starting at line 5, "The problem was --" and you're now referring to the Serbs - you said: "... the problem was that their pretensions were enormous and unrealistic. They wanted to control the cantonisation or, rather, they wanted to control a large part of the territories, especially those in which the Serbs were not predominant, and where the problems -- and there the problems arose." Can you describe a bit further for the Judge -- Judges what the problem was when you say they claimed areas in which the Serbs were not predominant.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, if you know that the Serbs were seeking control on the left bank of the river Neretva where their presence is almost symbolic. There were only 15 to 20 per cent Serbs in Stolac. The vast majority of the population were Croats and Muslim Bosniaks. Also, on the left bank of Mostar, not to mention Jablanica, Konjic, and other places. So the Serbs, who amounted to 31 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina and who had a little more in territorial terms, because their population was rural rather than urban so they controlled territory which was not densely inhabited but was large in area, however, they were not seeking those territories alone but also the towns, especially towns in which the Serbs were in a minority. They were not sincere in the negotiations about cantonisation. They put forward conditions to which we could not agree simply in order to raise tensions and complicate the situation. During those negotiations there were expulsions, murders, occupation of particular territories, and all this raised tensions. The aim of all this was to exert pressure on the negotiations and the reconstruction of Yugoslavia. In the Yugoslav constitution, there was a provision to the effect that the Yugoslav People's Army was, first of all, a people's army and, secondly, a guarantee of the survival of the state. At the time we are referring to, October, 1991, the army was no longer a people's army. It was a pro-fascist army. And secondly, it was no longer an army of all the nations and nationalities of Yugoslavia, as the phrase went. It was a Serbian, Montegnegrin, and Chetnik army. After what it did in Slovenia and especially in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so we can move forward. If you'd direct your attention to paragraph 5 of the same document, it says: "The decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the neutrality of Bosnia and Herzegovina is endorsed but with the condition that Bosnia and Herzegovina may not nor will it be a military training ground for continued aggression." Do we understand this document correct, sir -- correctly, sir, that on the 8th of October, 1991, the official policy of HDZ of BiH was that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be neutral in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very significant thing that the HDZ achieved at the time. The only thing we could ask, and we did ask for this in the Presidency, was that in the negotiations between Serbia and the JNA on the one hand and the Republic of Croatia on the other, Bosnia and Herzegovina should be at least neutral. This had a number of other consequences of significance for us Croats. Neutrality would mean that our soldiers, the soldiers of Bosnia-Herzegovina, should no longer go to the JNA, and we were successful in this. But the Serbs continued to go as volunteers. Also, what is especially important, we asked that neutrality imply that from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina one could not shell the Republic of Croatia. This was a permanent practice because the JNA was beyond the control of the civilian authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As you will see later on from the documents, two months later we held a meeting with the leadership of the JNA in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you direct your attention to the last page of this document, sir. Did you sign that document as president of the party?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving a few weeks forward, sir, to the 11th of November, 1991, was something called the Croatian Community of Bosnia Posavina created?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where was that territory located, the territory or municipalities that were claimed to comprise the Posavina community?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the northern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the most fertile part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where the Croats were in the majority, and we were in power in Bosanski Brod, in Derventa, in Bosanski Samac, participated in Brcko and Modrica, had absolute power in Odzak and Orasje, and this is an area that was later to suffer a great deal because it was on the contentious Belgrade-Banja Luka road. After the Travnik region and the Herzegovina region unified and we created the Sarajevo region, which never actually functioned, and then the Bihac region, which also never came to life, it was quite normal for the Croats from the areas of those municipalities to group together, to link up, to prepare themselves, and after the establishment of those other regions it was quite normal for there to be a Posavina region too. However, those who created the Posavina region were not ultimately thinking of the role to be played by that region when they all unified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, sir. I would like to ask the witness about the Posavina, just to refresh our memory concerning geography. I believe Posavina takes its name after the River Sava and it is south of -- the territory south of the Sava River, so I believe that it is what we are talking when we have that, particularly as you also said rather fertile territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is it right, sir, that it is south of Sava in that region where the Croats had -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honour. Precisely as you said, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, with the -- using the Sanction system, I'd like to show to the courtroom a map that was used during the opening statement, has been provided to all in the courtroom previously. If you can see that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you please confirm that the area marked there in the upper, one might say the north-east, corner of Bosnia and Herzegovina in blue, that was the territory claimed to comprise the community of the Bosanska Posavina.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the territory that comprised the party community of Bosanska Posavina. There are several municipalities in this territory too where the Croats are not in a majority. This did not represent any territorial pretensions, it was simply the party organisation, the task of which was to have the citizens associated together and prepared for the events that would follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I next ask you to look, please, at Exhibit P 00072. And let me direct you to pages 7 to 8, I believe, of the Croatian version. And in the English I believe the passages will be found at pages 7 and 8. If you can look, direct your attention, sir, to passage which starts with, "That we have contact with guy --" excuse me. Starting on page 7 of your version, I believe English version: "President, in reference to Bosnia, as I said at the previous meeting, we have also had a problem with the conduct of our people. Kljuic called me to say that he had heard that you have a contact with these guys from Herzegovina, that he is against that and I told him on the phone that any kind of actions --"

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. As we have received a large number of transcripts from various meetings along with this witness's testimony, I would like it first to be established whether the witness was present at this meeting and only then could he be asked what was said at the meeting and what he knows about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall a telephone conversation with President Tudjman of Croatia around the 14th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And tell us about that conversation.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After difficulties arose in communication, you have to bear in mind what the situation was in Sarajevo, which was encircled. The JNA and fascist Milosevic aggression against Croatia was culminating. Vukovar had been shelled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, for interrupting, but we don't have that document on the monitors. We know what it's about because we've seen it, but the accused also don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Registrar, could we have the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I -- if I understood the question, which I believe was a proper one, Mr. Scott was asking the witness if he recalled the conversation and now the witness was testifying from memory as opposed to what is in the document, and I would prefer that the witness not look at the document to refresh his memory because obviously he's indicated that he -- he remembers that conversation. So, you know, we would like to have his memory as opposed to something that's -- that's being paraphrased by President Tudjman as to what purportedly was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Before refreshing his memory, perhaps the witness could talk to us about the telephone conversation that took place on the 14th of November, 1991. Witness, please answer this question which all and everybody has in mind. You told us that there had been a telephone conversation with Mr. Tudjman, and you were in Sarajevo at the time. Could you tell us what the background of the telephone conversation was, and what did you tell Mr. Tudjman, and what did he tell you? And then we will check this out with the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to say to counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not -- you are responding to the Bench, not to the attorney.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, Your Honour, my memory's relatively very good, so it's not about checking my memory, but the fact is I spoke to President Tudjman on a daily basis. From the text before me, I know what this is about. When I was starting to tell you what the situation in Croatia was like and what the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was like, a large number of officials of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina were no longer seeking replies to their questions in Sarajevo but in Zagreb. At that time, I said to President Tudjman, "Don't receive them. Send them to me in Sarajevo. Let's maintain the party discipline," because the worst thing was that 99 per cent of them couldn't reach President Tudjman. They reached low-level officials in Zagreb, who made their own suggestions to them, which were often contrary to the overall policy of the HDZ, both in Zagreb and in Sarajevo. These were difficulties, but of course as there were changes in the overall policies, these people in Zagreb were happy to have these lads coming over and saying, "We are very eager." So as the president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was asking that they not be received in Zagreb on an individual basis but that the policy be agreed with me and that they be sent to Sarajevo. However, most of them didn't want to go to Sarajevo. They wanted to go to Zagreb. They had personal connections there, family connections, friends, and so on, and this led to confusion on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told him that, and what did he answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vaguely, because he liked them to go there. They arrived there with huge enthusiasm, saying, "We have only one president, President Tudjman, and no one else." And those people in Zagreb didn't really understand Bosnia. Many of them didn't even love Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you and President Tudjman discussed the formation of these regional communities?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were to support the forming of the regional communities in the way that I described yesterday; subordination, political directives, work on the ground, linking up. At that time we were having problems with children evading military service, we were having problems with the educational system. Many children had not enrolled in school. Many were unable to do so, to enroll in school and university. Then we had problems with vaccines for children, treatment of patients with serious illnesses, and a part of the Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina were participating in the defence of Croatia. And this refers not just to Croats but also to Bosniak Muslims. They needed medical treatment too. We had a lot of problems with the reuniting of families. If somebody who was wounded in Croatia who came from Bosnia, the family had to go to Croatia. So that these communities were justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had you indicated to President Tudjman that you disagreed with the formation of these regional communities?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I said was that the Presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina ultimately supported the communities but in the function that I explained to you, because there were no intimations at that time that they would have any ambitions towards any statehood and creating states. So in this war danger, that was a very good move, to link up and associate because -- for subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said there were no intimations at that time that there -- that they would have any ambitions towards statehood. Are you saying you did not make any such intimations or that nobody, no one made such intimations?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody did publicly, and I didn't do so publicly or otherwise. It never entered my head. I couldn't have imagined anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, who did -- who did so not publicly?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in seven days, or three or four days, the formation of Herceg-Bosna was to follow, and when it was established, it wasn't expressly political or nor did it have expressly statehood attributes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, on line 19, you just said, "Well, nobody did publicly ..." A fair implication of your answer, sir, is that there may have been some who did so not publicly, and I'm asking you again, can you identify anyone who did look at these groupings as a move toward para-states or statehood, whether they expressed these views publicly or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, gentlemen, who thought what. Just like you, I was to learn all about it in due course, with the developments as they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you're telling the Judges that as of the fall of 1991, in the midst of everything that we've talked about since yesterday, you had no idea that there were certain individuals within the party who had different views about these matters than you did?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, to the form of the question. That is not what the gentleman stated, and it mischaracterises his testimony. I suggest Mr. Scott rephrase the question to reflect exactly what the gentleman indicated, because the questions and answers are rather different than the one now that he's suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't agree, Your Honour. The witness just said on line 6 and 7, "Just like you -" presumably referring to me - "I was to learn all about it in due course," meaning apparently the implication as of the 18th of October, he didn't -- or 8th of October, he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He can ask what he learned and then we might be able to carry on a conversation from there. I think there are a lot of suggestions, or there's too much reading into the answers by the Prosecutor. If we go step-by-step; who, what, where, why, how, and describe and explain, we'll get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I'll ask you this way: When did you first learn that there were people within the HDZ party that had a different view on the state nature of these regional bodies and the ambitions towards statehood? When did you first learn there were people in the party who had such views?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I object to the form of the question. He's never indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're not going to waste time. What we're interested in as Judges is to know what actually happened. We're not in an American trial. This is a mixed type of trial, and it is in the interests of the Judges to learn what happened on the political level, what actually happened. We have one of the principal actors here who was there at the time and who held responsible posts within the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so this witness is best placed to tell us what from his point of view he saw and how he saw that evolution taking place. So, sir, you attended this debate between -- going on between the Prosecution and the Defence. We as Judges are not going to take part in the debate. What we want to learn is the truth and the manifestation of the truth, and it is the witness who is to enlighten us on that point. So we have just learnt that we have the constitution, there was the constitution of an entity, the establishment of a geographical entity within the scope of creating a region, and that region was Posavina, the Sava River valley. And now the question for us Judges is you, at the head of the HDZ party, you experienced and lived through all that, so was there a consensus amongst the party members as -- were you in the minority, or did you represent the majority? So could you give us a series of explanations to help us understand this. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The foundation of the Posavina community was a natural course along the sense of which the Presidency of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina insisted upon, that people link up in resolving problems ranging from education through medicine and further afield. However, nobody knew that those communities would one day unite to form a new association. I especially did not know this as president of the Croatian Democratic Union, for instance. I was not even called to attend that establishment on the 18th of November. However, in that particular formulation, as that was put, there was nothing especially dangerous or threatening. What was dangerous was that we did that after the Serbs, because the Serbs had already formed SAO Krajina and were actually working in a destructive manner within Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. So it was no longer a question of the war in Croatia, which was being fought through and was becoming a bloody one, but the problem was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When this Herceg-Bosna community was established, from that point on I received assurances that that was quite normal and that it was a fact -- in fact a continuation of the regional unification with the same problems and subject matter. And as I lived in Sarajevo and represented the HDZ, I had, the very next day, to answer questions put to me by journalists at a press conference and say was that a parallel of what the Serbs were doing and then what the Croats were doing and that the Bosniaks should continue along the same course? As a politician I said, well, no, that's not what it's like, people. It's just to help each other out and to see that everything goes -- develops well. But they were to have meetings without me very shortly after that. In fact, on the 24th, I believe. It was the 24th of December. And the key meeting was to be held on the 27th of December in Zagreb where, quite openly for the first time, everybody presented their views. And I, to be quite frank, was left in the minority there. And the finale came on the 2nd of February, 1992, when we parted ways, of course with the very tragic consequences that this had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your position, and you've just described it to us, what motivated the fact that you were apprehensive? You had this apprehension. What caused it? Was it the parallel that drew with the SAO Krajina, perhaps? So what allowed you to have concerns on that score?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's quite simple. First of all, they separated from the legal leadership in Sarajevo and contacted people from the periphery in Zagreb, which had already shown themselves to be extremists. Vice Vukojevic, for example, had more influence, wielded more influence on the HDZ policy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the field than did the legal leadership. The second point is this: In the psychological sense with those citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who already at that time were the victims of a situation of that kind, any attempts - and this was interpreted in the Sarajevo press which was pro-Serb oriented - as an attempt on the part of the Croats to take their own portion, whereas that wasn't true nor was it realistic because you could have seen in the list of municipalities in the communities there were only 5 per cent of Croats there. So they had no chance of ruling over that area, taking control of that area. So that then caused, among the Muslims as well, a feeling of jeopardy. What did that mean? Were they supposed to make their own communities, to establish their own communities? And that was the best road to destroying Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the other hand, as somebody who lived his whole life within a specific code of conduct, I asked them if they were dissatisfied and if they didn't wish to support -- lend their support to the policy that we had already adopted at the convention in Mostar, then I said to them, Gentlemen, go ahead, let's draw up a new convention, and you can voice a new platform. And if you win a majority for that kind of policy, then put it into practice and find a new president. So what -- why I was irritated and felt aggrieved was that we within the frameworks of a legally adopted political platform on the ground, thanks to individuals who were the leaders in those communities, that they started implementing quite the opposite policy of the one proclaimed. Had it been along the lines of progress and defence, that wouldn't have been tragic, but it was tragic because it went along the lines of further toppling and destroying the principles of Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence. And that came to the fore at the meeting in Zagreb. It all came out there. And after that meeting, as I've already said, I left, although I stayed on until the 2nd of February when a Plenary session was convened by the people in Zagreb. At the time I had two options, one not to go, and then they could out-vote and vote on anything; and the second was to go there and to attend and to fight for what I wanted to see go through. As you know, the Plenary Session was interrupted and they were not able to put through their ideas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you. Thank you for giving us those numerous explanations and details. A question comes to me. After November, when you saw this movement being created, these developments, why as you -- you as president of the HDZ, did you not at that point in time call a meeting of the HDZ, the top echelons of the HDZ, to take a stand rather than allowing these developments to take place after the Zagreb meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and because a convention could not be held at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the HDZ statute and provisions didn't allow for the convocation of a convention? Do you have to have a certain number of members who want to call a convention? You said yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, everything was possible according to the rules and provisions of the statute. The statute did provide the possibility of me being able to collect a certain number of signatures and convene a convention, but for practical reasons everything was blocked, so people couldn't come to the meeting. So you -- as you were able to see, this second meeting was held in Zagreb. We came from all parts. I came by plane via Austria, then went by car from Austria to Zagreb. Others went via Dalmatia and Rijeka to reach Zagreb, whereas we in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because of the blockades, the SAO Krajinas, we were not able to rally enough people and have them come to Bosnia-Herzegovina. So legally speaking, I did have the possibility of doing that. There were a sufficient number of delegates who would lend their support, but in practical terms, because of the danger of war, we couldn't hold the meeting in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It wasn't physically feasible. They couldn't reach the area because everything was blocked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could have the witness please be shown Exhibit P 00078, which is in the second bundle. We've now finished the first bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as soon as you have that document can you tell us, please -- can you look at that document and is that a record of the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it would appear, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Article I says: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be established as a political, cultural, economic and territorial whole." And in Article II it lists the municipalities which will comprise the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And turning to the end of the document, do you see that it was Mate Boban who either signed or whose name -- the document is over his name? Over his name?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The title given to Mr. Boban in this document is president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We know from yesterday that he had been the -- by this time the first vice-president of the party. When did he become the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume when they were constituted. I wasn't there. I wasn't invited to attend, and even if I were, I wouldn't have gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why weren't you invited?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would have to ask them that, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said if you had been invited, you wouldn't have gone. Why not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't have gone because with respect to the legal HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a political party that represented 95 per cent of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this was a parallel organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But surely you must have seen this as a very important development among the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way, but you needn't. It doesn't have to be put that way. If you look at the way the community was constituted and the number of municipalities mentioned - Bugojno, Jablanica, Konjic - that was very unrealistic, impossible propositions. But you know when people say, We're all going, let's all go, then you'll see in the minutes that individuals from those provinces say, Ah, young men are brimming over with enthusiasm and things like that, but that was the wrong move. Although it was a very skilful move because it says political, cultural, economic, and so on and so forth. There is no mention of administrative separatist state or anything like that. None of those attributes. So I had to defend that for political reasons that, in formal terms, yes, they had joined -- they had united, but nobody would know that the developments would have been such that this was actually to take root.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said just a moment ago, you said if we -- if you look at the way the community was constituted and the number of municipalities - you mentioned several, including Jablanica and Konjic - why was that unrealistic and impossible?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: Those communities were established to begin with as HDZ communities. That means as party communities, which were supposed to rally people, Croats first and foremost, to see to their needs, to look after them, and so on. After these communities united, the Croatian democratic communities into regional ones, this is -- became a new form of unification of association, and it was one level higher, a higher level of association. But the formula that it was cultural, economic, and so on, that kind of community, that still was not against the law, and it wasn't -- didn't present a danger to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. Why was it unrealistic and impossible to include Jablanica and Konjic in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because the absolute majority population was the Muslim population. That did not belong either culturally, politically, or in terms of where they lived to those communities. It's just like if you co-opted Sardinia, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look at Article 8, you say there was nothing about any administrative ambitions or executive government ambitions. Article 8 says: "The Presidency of the community shall appoint the executive and administrative bodies of authority in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna," does it not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see Article 8. Would you scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the assistance of the registry, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an attempt to turn this kind of community into executive power ultimately, into an executive authority, and that is what made it unacceptable as far as I was concerned, because at that time we had power and authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, legitimately elected authorities. Now, the fact that it wasn't functioning in certain parts, that was because the situation was as it was. The presence of the Yugoslav People's Army, for example, drawing parallels with the Serb side. But the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina still existed, and its regular executive powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll go next, please, to Exhibit P 00082.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Before we do that, let's stay with this document. Witness, I can see the preamble of this decision, which was taken on the 18th of November, as it says, 1991, and in the preamble it states that that decision was adopted by the representatives -- elected representatives of the Croatian people. How many of them were there, these individuals who met to take this decision, to the best of your knowledge? Because there must have been HDZ members, must there not, attending that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact number, but most probably they were local presidents of municipalities, deputies in parliament from that area, local deputies or MPs, and certain officers who probably held some posts in the state administration on behalf of the HDZ but who went down there. I don't know. I never actually saw a list of those who were present, the names of the people who attended. But the fact is that they were HDZ members, and most of them had been elected, at least at a lower level, at the elections held in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you told us that you didn't -- you weren't invited to attend that meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you learn of what had happened at the meeting and of the decisions that had been taken? Did you know about it the same day, the next day, several days later? When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, I never learnt everything that had taken place, but that same night there was a television broadcast. The television announced that the community had been formed and the president was Mate Boban, MA, and the following day journalists came to see me and asked me how that had happened, how they were able to do that when I was not there. I tried to make less of it, but quite obviously they had great pretensions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would just like to draw your attention to the fact that this decision and the text was amended on the 3rd of January, 1992. So it is not the integral test -- text of what was stated on the 18th of November, and if the witness needs to explain what helped -- what happened in 1991, I'd like you to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that point there is an earlier version of the document which was intended to be included in the bundle. Unfortunately, the wrong document was included, but we'll provide that to you as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a question from one of my colleagues, the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, staying with the document that we've just been discussing on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, if we read Article 5 of the document - I have the English text - the community shall respect the legitimately elected bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, Article 7, it says the Presidency shall be the organ, the legislative organ, of the community, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise but they don't have the exact text in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you explain to us, please, whether Article 7 in your opinion gave legislative powers to the Presidency which was to a certain extent in contradiction with powers democratically elected of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Or in the opposite case, whether these two provisions are completely legal, complementary, and logical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decisions following on from these two articles were not legal and could not have been registered at the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They came in through the back door, so to speak, introducing some para-organisation which had pretensions of having absolute executive powers. What does this mean, that the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna are made up of the Croatian people in the municipal authorities and from among the Croatian Defence Council? That's very broad, with no legal provisions and instruments. On the other hand, the very fact that Herceg-Bosna wanted to nominate executive powers and authorities is contrary to the constitutional set-up of the state as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have just observed that the document we have on our screens or, rather, on Exhibit 78, Exhibit 78 is a document which, according to the preamble, was brought up-to-date on the 3rd of July, 1993. So this document, as Counsel Alaburic noted, was not the original document of the 18th of November, 1991, because in the preamble it is stated that this decision was amended on the 3rd of July, 1992. So this is the final draft that we're looking at, that we have before us. But this draft is dated 1992, not 1991. Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the registry could please display Exhibit 79, P 00079, which will not be in the bundle. It will not be in the hard copy because, by error, it was not included. I see the Croatian language version on my screen, but I assume that people who need to see it in English can. We can put an English version on the ELMO if we have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We -- it's going to come up in English, because for the time being we have the Croatian version on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it's coming up now, if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the Croatian language version that was just put on your screen, now do you see that document?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Thank you. Yes, I have it in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we can go back to the English version. Please display for the Judges in particular, in case there's any questions about the similarity of language between the two versions. I'd like the Judges -- can you scroll down and show, for example, Article 1. Article 2. In reference to the Judge's question, can you show Article 5? Can the registry please also display Exhibit P 00077.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we just see the whole document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. And if there's another -- keep continuing to the end of the document, please, if counsel can see that. We'll stop at any point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Article 7 seems to be rather different than the one that's displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The 1992 version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go back to Article 7, please. Can you enlarge that? Yes. Correct. Can you also then go to Exhibit P 00077.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we go along, would the gentleman concede that Article 7 is different? And perhaps can he comment on it if he has any comments, I don't know. Because this would have been the version, apparently, that he would have seen at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So we can see that, as far as Article 7 is concerned, it's not the same in both documents. Do you have any comments to make, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never read another version of Article 7, nor was it available to me. I lived in occupied Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you say that the Article 7 which we have on our screen is something you did not know about in Sarajevo. Now, today, in 2006, what is your assessment of this Article you see today, Article 7 and Article 7 which you read in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the translation, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a language problem here. So what you have on your screen now in your own language is the text, the original text which goes back to 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On two screens I have the identical text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps it might be easier if we gave the gentleman a hard copy at least of the latter version, the 1992 version. That might assist him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While this is happening, Your Honour, if I could have a point of clarification. Is the gentleman asserting today, as I understood him to say, that he did not see any of these documents because he was in occupied Sarajevo? Is that his testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The question that has been put to you, which I shall put to you now, this text which you have before you is a text which you knew nothing about when you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This document which we have before us is a document which you discovered at what point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I never read it nor was I interested in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means that you are seeing it for the first time in its original version; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't seen it yet, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you've got it here before you right now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I have before me is two identical texts from the first version of the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the best would be to place on the ELMO the 1991 document. Is that something you can do, Registrar? Registrar, let's put the 1991 document on the ELMO, namely Exhibit 79. You don't have it? The Prosecution, do you have a hard copy of this document? So we shall keep document 79 on the screen and put number 78 on the ELMO so that the witness can compare the two. Could the usher put number 78 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I shall hand over my copy. Here you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a B/C/S version. Let's turn to Article 7. You need to turn the page. Here we are. So you have both texts in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of comment would you like to make regarding these two texts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm no legal expert, so I cannot tell you what the legal difference is, but as a citizen who was involved in these matters, at first glance I can tell you that beside the president and two vice-presidents, there is now also a president and a Presidency composed of officials and representatives of the Croatian people at municipal level, and so on. And also that the Presidency's a legislative body. So it's supposed to replace a parliament, speaking as a layperson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are telling us that in the document you have before you, Article 7, this is a document dated 1992, you explained that there is a judiciary that has been established. That is a remark you have just made. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just moment. Just moment, please. [Interpretation] I said that as a layperson, not as an expert. So please don't draw any conclusions from what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before -- before we give the floor back to Mr. Scott, Your Honour, perhaps we could have a point of clarification. The gentleman expressed certain views prior -- once he saw the 1992 version. It was -- it was then pointed out to him that there was a 1991 version, at which point we learned that he never saw the versions, either the 1991 or 1992 at the time, never read them. The point of clarification would be when he was giving that explanation, on what basis was he giving the explanation if he didn't see the documents and this is the first time, and especially now that he admits he's not a jurist and doesn't know how to read such documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. He made a negative sign with his hand. Could you add something to what -- to what has just been said, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document from 1991 was published in the newspapers, and I saw that document. I never saw the document from 1992. Secondly, I don't know what this has to do with the trial. This gentleman says I'm not a lawyer. Well, that's what I said. But to understand the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you only have to be a normal person, you don't always need to be an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So in light of all you've said so far, you are adding something new. You say that the 1991 document was published in the press, in the media; is that right? That's what you've just said. And that the 1992 document is something you are seeing for the first time today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, we have quarter of an hour left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can go to Exhibit P 00082. I'm sorry. My apology. If we can pull up -- if the registry can please -- my apology. If the registry can please pull up Exhibit P 00079. It's not in the bundle, but in light of questions that have been asked. Mr. President, as I said -- as I said about two minutes ago, it was indeed -- indeed the case that another version of the 1991 document was to have been the appropriate exhibit, and I apologise for the confusion that's been caused, but I will present that document in hard copy after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said you saw the 1991 document in the newspaper the next day -- I don't believe this is Exhibit 77. Can you go to the last page? Is this Exhibit 77? Sorry. Sir, if you can look at this document, and if you just look at that long enough to identify it, and if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be a mistake in the transcript. It's Exhibit number 79 and not 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise. This -- what we're looking at on the screen now should be Exhibit 77, which is what I see on the screen, is in fact what I recognise to be Exhibit 77, but you're right if I misspoke. What I'd like to the registry to display at the moment is 77. If you could display that, please. The English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll look at that, sir, yourself in the Croatian language version while we're also showing the courtroom the English version. Sir, if you've had a chance to read those two paragraphs, can you tell the Judges whether those -- whether those two additional paragraphs were also printed in the newspaper the day after the Assembly on the 18th of November, or in some days after that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. A lot of time has elapsed, but the content certainly fits within that context and most probably corresponds to what was published. So this is probably true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could we go on to Exhibit P 00085, then -- or 82. 82. Which should be back in the bundle, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as soon as you have that on your screen can you confirm that these -- that this is the record of a meeting of the Presidency of the HDZ BiH on the 28th of November, 1991, 10 days after the founding of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this meeting you did attend?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And chaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so that everyone can see that, under "Agenda" after the five items of the agenda, does the document say, sir, "The session was opened and chaired by the president, Stjepan Kljuic"? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Under the five items of the agenda -- there's an agenda listing five items. Immediately below item number 5, do you see the language that says: "The session was opened and chaired by the president, Stjepan Kljuic"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to the last page of the document in the Croatian-language version. Does it bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you will direct your attention to item -- paragraph c. There's item 1, and then there's a number of lettered paragraphs. If I can direct your attention to item 1.c, does the document say the following: "The Presidency of the BH HDZ unanimously adopts the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna of 18 November, 1991"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe you testified a moment ago that you didn't really care what this document was about, but did you give it your endorsement on the 28th of November, 1991, when you chaired this meeting? It says it was unanimously approved.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should know the context in which this was done. They had already established this Herceg-Bosna and now they had arrived and they already had the majority among the members of the Presidency who were there, so what was I supposed to do? To say let's have a vote and they would out-vote me, and then they would be legitimate. In the form in which they put it, culturally, economic, and so on, this was no threat to the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. By endorsing it I had to cover some weaknesses within the party as the president of the party. But except superficially, it had nothing in common with the Serbian SAO Krajinas. It didn't have any negative connotations. It didn't have any administrative political ambitions at that point in time. And of course I was making compromises. I accepted this because, as you can see, the Presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina was still the highest party body in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By the end of November, 1991, sir, had you lost control of the party?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the state institutions and official policy and negotiations with the international community, the answer is no. But as regards decisions made on the ground, especially in particular municipalities in the Travnik and Herzegovina region, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while Mr. Scott is looking, perhaps he could also look at item b, where it says there has been no split. Was that a political compromise? Was that a fabrication or somewhat of a kind way of putting it? What exactly does that mean? Because if you read b, then you go to c, perhaps you might understand why it was unanimous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was going to go back to that exact point, Mr. Karnavas. I think there will be cross-examination, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But let me just ask you, sir: You said you had to make compromises, but indeed b says, "There has been no split nor have there been any personal conflicts in the party leadership." But if I understand your testimony at line 17 of page 34, you agreed, sir, that by this time you had lost control of the party apparatus in at least the Travnik and regional -- and Herzegovina regions; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So despite what it says here, in fact there had been a split. There was a split.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was. But should this have been made public? Should the confusion of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina have been increased? Should our nervousness been conveyed to the ordinary citizens, the grassroots people, those in mixed marriages, those who wanted there to be peace? We had to put up a front of unity, and I wanted that. But over the next few months events would take a different course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So if I may take the break to have a confirming question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In fact, you yourself also were acting unrealistically in the way in that you had hopes that the party could remain together and the state, Bosnia and Herzegovina could be get -- got together where in fact this cohesion was crumbling under your feet, as it were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you one thing. My political platform, my legality was to fight for an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina and the equality of the Croatian people. There had been no official change in the party policy, but on the ground there had been behaviour which was contrary to this. Everything that the Serbs had temporarily occupied didn't mean that there would be no Bosnia-Herzegovina. One had to be serious when making political analyses. Kuwait was occupied but it didn't disappear. The government went into exile and later on it was liberated. There was no reason at the time to believe that Bosnia and Herzegovina would fail and disappear, and it turned out that I was right when I trusted the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to understand your position correctly. You weren't opposed to this decision as it has been mentioned that it was taken unanimously, even though you did tell us that in some municipalities there could be no political or cultural entity given the ethnic composition. Jablanica, Prozor, and Konjic are the ones you mentioned. Despite that -- this fact, you accept this decision. You accept it because you felt this would pose no threat, or is it that you realised at this stage that this might cause problems in the future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said that Prozor was a minority Croatian municipality. Prozor had the majority Croatian population. But until the point when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna announced the takeover of executive power, it was neither dangerous nor illegal. The moment that those people expressed ambitions to take over executive power wherever they could in parallel with the legal power, that's where there was a problem that would lead to disaster. On the other hand, when these communities were formed, which included Croats from some municipalities where we were not well represented or in the majority, all this was normal. But when communities were formed with ambitions to take over executive power, even in those municipalities where we were in the minority or approximately with the same level of representation as the Muslims, such as in Travnik and Bugojno, there problems would arise. I could have caused a scandal and said this is illegal, unlawful, counter-constitutional, it's against the party platform, but in view of my elections results within the party, I believed that the people from areas where the Croats had co-existed with other peoples would act in such a way that the situation would calm down, especially as in parallel with these events the war in Croatia ended, in the Republic of Croatia. You have to know that on the 2nd of January, 1992, in Sarajevo, peace was signed between the JNA, the rebel Serbs, and the legitimate authorities of the Republic of Croatia. There was a tendency for a general calming down of the situation, and it did not suit us to create division in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. It is now 10.30. We shall have to have our technical break, and we shall resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to go on working until 12.30 in this second sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, just one point of clarification before moving on to the next exhibit. You said several times before the break that as you understand this organisation, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, you didn't see -- and we've all heard that you're not a lawyer, but you didn't see anything illegal about it. Were you aware or did you become aware at some point that the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina had declared Herceg-Bosna illegal?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was completely something that was expected when they had ambitions of taking over executive power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I next ask for the witness to be shown Exhibit P 00089.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I -- may I still ask a question for the previous matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What we all notice is -- is unsatisfactory and difficult to understand with Herceg-Bosna is that there are, I think, four municipalities included, which all have a different -- or had a different majority than Croat. Absolute majorities of Serbs in Kupres and absolute majority of Muslims in Gornji Vakuf, Konjic, and Jablanica. Was that an issue? Were there discussions about this or was this simply for geographical reasons, probably because one wanted to have a link to the south, accepted without much discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The session where we accepted Herceg-Bosna, there were no detailed analyses that had been made, because the principle of associating with party members and people in the area to look after their interests. No other principles were declared at that point in time in geographical terms. I can't agree that the Croats were in the minority in Kupres and Gornji Vakuf. There was an equal number of Croats and Serbs in Kupres, whereas in Gornji Vakuf an equal number of Croats and Muslims. But in Bugojno and Travnik, for example, there was just a slight majority of Muslims compared to the Croats, whereas in Jablanica and Konjic the absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, following up on Judge Trechsel's question, sir, and on this point, did you ever advise other people in the Croatian leadership, either in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Zagreb, that given what you've just said, you expected the Muslims to oppose Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you must know that before that the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina had proclaimed unconstitutional the Serbian Krajinas that they had made, and then Herceg-Bosna too. And in all the talks that I had at the time with President Tudjman and other officials from Zagreb, I tried to show them that they shouldn't irritate the Bosniak Muslims who at that point in time were our only political friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can now ask you to look at Exhibit P 00089.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this particular instance, Mr. President, because this is a lengthy transcript, I think for the witness it will much easier for him to work with a hard copy than trying to go from page to page in the electronic version, if I could suggest that. If we can just have a minute, Your Honour. Sorry, Your Honour, it would be easier if we just isolate the B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as you look at that document, is it correct that on the 27th of December, 1991, you and a number of other senior representatives or officials of both the HDZ BH, the -- of Herceg-Bosna and of the Croatian government, this group of people met with President Tudjman on the 27th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At President Tudjman's residence on Pantovcak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what you understood the purpose of this meeting was, why had this group of people been called together at that particular moment in time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you already know, we weren't able to draw up an HDZ convention or -- of HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or a meeting, a convention in any Bosnia-Herzegovinian town because of the circumstances that prevailed. We weren't able to hold a convention. On the other hand, the regional communities, through their conduct and actions, did not find favour with part of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was quite clear at that point in time that we had two parallel formations on the Croatian political arena: One was the legal one, the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whose president I was, and the people who were elected to parliament and then the executive organs of power and authority. The other side was the one led by Mate Boban. Whereas we from the leadership of the Croatian Democratic Union did not exclude the activities of Herceg-Bosna, the leadership of Herceg-Bosna for its part absolutely and in practical terms denied the existence of the legal leadership of the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking, sir, at the first page --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Just a moment, please. [Interpretation] In Zagreb, among the influential people, there was no uniform way of thinking either, so that this meeting was convened in an extraordinary situation in order to reformulate or support the present policy, the policy up until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know who among the senior Croatian officials, State of Croatia officials, other than President Tudjman, were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please say so.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the minister -- Minister Susak. He was already defence minister at the time. Then the vice-premier, Mr. Milan Ramljak. HDZ Presidency member of Croatia, academician Miroslav Brozovic. Then there was Josip Manolic, the former Prime Minister, and there were several other lower-ranking officials from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I can direct your attention to the first page and the first portion attributed to President Tudjman. You see, sir, that he opens the meeting: "Gentlemen, this meeting is open. I welcome our guest, an HDZ delegation from Bosnia-Herzegovina, with whom we are going to talk about an issue currently of the greatest importance for Croatia." And continuing on down through that section and right before you get to a section referring to -- you'll see the names Milosevic and Gligorov. Before that, President Tudjman continues to say, "What our position will be with regard to the Croatian part of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And is what is stated here, sir, your understanding of what the topics, what the agenda of the meeting was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that point in time it was quite certain that the Republic of Croatia, together with the Republic of Slovenia, had gained international recognition, and that official ceremony or act was to take place 19 days later. However, the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina hadn't been resolved yet. And quite obviously there were a number of variants and options and expectations, and more clearly than ever before there would be division between the leadership of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina and those who were in favour of an independent integral Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the other side who saw their chance in Bosnia's division, Bosnia-Herzegovina's division.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the end of the section I just referred you to a moment ago, President Tudjman says, "Mr. Kljuic, you have the floor." And then "Stjepan Kljuic," and then you begin to talk, which goes on for, as we will see, for some pages of transcript. If I can ask you to go to page 3 of the document, of your transcript, there's a paragraph where you say: "For us and for the HDZ there were no dilemmas in this respect because this was our party's platform as well and we stated our position clearly a year ago that we were for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina as long as there was a shred of a chance that it may come to pass." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. When you talk here about the party's platform, are you talking about the original platform on which the party was elected in 1990? Is that the platform you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll go to page 7 of the transcript. There's a portion where -- paragraph where you're talking about party discipline, and in that paragraph you go on to say, if you can find this: "I think this is a difficult time and whatever we agree upon tonight, whatever positions we take here will have to be implemented. Whoever is not prepared to adhere to this, myself included, fine, let them step down. Let them make sure they follow the Croatian course, which is the most important one strategically." Does this statement indicate what we've been talking about this morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. It's leading in nature and it's very unhelpful to the Trial Chamber. He can ask the gentleman what did he mean. He uttered those words. He ought to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karnavas is premature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you mean, sir, when you said this had been a difficult time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were difficult times. That's the first point. Secondly, I wanted us to have a joint line or course. I had my own platform, of course, which until then was the official one, and I said if we agree, then we must all obey what we have agreed. And I knew that if we were to agree to what they had said, I would be disobedient and I would have to go. So I tried to gain support from President Tudjman for everything we have done thus far jointly and for the programme orientation that was official one of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll go to page 8 of the transcript, you will see a paragraph that says: "Therefore ..." At the end of the paragraph, it says, "But in any case we should prepare alternative solutions like when we met here on St. Ante's --" I'm sorry, I don't know if the translation is correct -- "Day and prepared three alternative solutions." Can you tell the Judges about this earlier meeting referenced here on that day and what three alternative solutions were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to be -- to obstruct the -- but perhaps the gentleman could just give us a narration of what he recalls what he said, and so on and so forth, to put this matter into context. The reason I say this is now we're going and taking snippets out of this transcript, and we either go through his entire presentation, otherwise we're just getting bits and pieces and it's very difficult to create a record this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if Mr. Karnavas would like us to read the entire transcript into the record, I'm happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's up to the Prosecutor to decide how he wishes to do his direct examination. I'm merely trying to help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for your help, sir. How would you like to proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you intend to go through the whole document or -- do you want to go through the whole document or certain points of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it's fair to accuse anyone of taking something out of context when the entire courtroom has the entire document in front of them, and the Judges, the Defence counsel, the accused themselves, everybody in this courtroom can read the entire document for themselves. But if Mr. Karnavas would like, we can take the time to read the entire document out loud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Karnavas, a short time ago you also interfered willy-nilly and criticised the Prosecutor because he had put the question in a certain way, and you suggested that he should ask, What did you mean by that? Now, that's exactly what he's asking now, and I must say I cannot find fault with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would agree to one -- to what extent. When we're talking something out of context, and I dare say it's out of context, when he's just reading one portion of it, there's a whole discussion, I believe the witness here is saying a lot throughout this period, because he's giving explanations, he's giving his positions. And to simply take a matter and say, What did you mean? without knowing what he said before that point is very difficult to follow. So when I do my cross-examination, I don't have a problem going page by page, line by line. It will take a long time. I merely wish the witness to give us a narration or at least a general feeling of what it was that they discussed, and then when we get to these three points, at least I will know exactly what it is that is being conveyed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I would think that we are all able to build the bridges, having the document and all being professionals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would also like to ask the following, that I believe that it would be really very important to listen to the witness about that -- those alternatives which he referred to in this paper. And when he said, and I quote, "I think we should wait. We should come to an agreement. But in any case we should prepare alternative solutions like when we met here on St. Ante's Day and prepared three alternative solutions." I really believe that it would be good for the Bench, good for the Defence, and go for every one of us here if we would listen and know about these alternative solutions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, in light of the guidance that the Judges have given us, can we start, please, by point of reference, and there's a reference to St. Ante's Day. Can you tell us what day in the calendar that is?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 13th of June, and they were one of the two major meetings in Zagreb, and I attended on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this is the 13th of June meeting that we discussed yesterday, and you said -- you say here --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- on that day and prepared three alternative solutions. So we weren't able to get that from you yesterday, but could you please tell the Judges now what the three alternative solutions were discussed on the 13th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
