utterances.text: Well, the first was a confederation for Yugoslavia. The second was, above all, an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina. And third, there were two points: One, if there was a division of territory, that the Croats and Muslim Bosniaks should go together with Croatia; and B, if there was this general division of Bosnia, that every entity should take its part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on the 13th of June, 1991, did you express a view in favour of any particular of those three solutions?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was in favour of an integral, sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. When we go back and look at the three alternatives - I'm looking on page 47, line 3 - it says the first was a confederation for Yugoslavia. Can you tell us a bit more about what that would have been; when you say that, what you mean.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the hegemony of the Belgrade regime and Slobodan Milosevic himself, the republics in the former Yugoslavia called for autonomy up to the level permitted under the 1974 constitution. There were proposals voiced, and this was discussed with the European Union here in The Hague, according to which the federal state of Yugoslavia should have five joint functions, and they would be the army, the police, finance, then there was the civil or civilian, the water communications, and a common currency, which means that in all other departments the republics would enjoy autonomy and independence. Apart from the political problems, there was the financial problem that was very marked in Yugoslavia, because the resources gained by the republics were not equally distributed. And I'll illustrate this by a short example. Croatia, for instance, had the ship-building industry, which at the time was the sixth largest ship-building industry in the world. It ranked sixth, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're going far afield. We're not talking about ship building here. And before we lose -- we're losing it now on the transcript on the screen, you said the third, there were two points: "One, if there was a division of territory, that the Croats and Muslim Bosniaks should go together with Croatia; and B, if there was this general division of Bosnia, that every entity should take its part." So do we understand correctly when you talk about a third option or a third possibility, there were two variants; there was variant A and variant B, if you will?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you can't follow what I'm saying if you're just looking for, under point 3, A and B, variants or alternatives A and B. You must know what the process was. On the 27th of December, at the meeting in Zagreb, there was no longer the possibility of having a confederation for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Croatia and Slovenia had already stepped down from the federation at that time. The situation had changed completely. Their positions had changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Two alternatives remaining on the table, sir, is it correct, is for an integral, sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, indivisible; and the second option was either some entity that would go with Croatia or an entity that would completely divide -- be divided into separate ethnic entities. Are those the two options that existed at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Concerning those two existing options, again as I asked you earlier - perhaps we will get to it - did you tell people in this meeting that you did not expect the Muslims to agree to a joint organisation with the Croats in this scenario?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Muslims never agreed. Later on, with developments, they even signed some sort of split agreement between the -- between President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic. There would be a proposal for a confederation. But that never took root, never actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to page 12 of the transcript. You will find this paragraph, or passage, on the page, please: "I think it would be acceptable to have a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina divided into cantons which would guarantee human rights to all, et cetera. But to partition Bosnia according to the Serbian recipe would put us into minority position as we constitute over 50 per cent in 14 municipalities while in five municipalities we have a plurality." Does that further confirm, sir, what you've told to the Judges yesterday and today in terms of the status of the Croat majorities in certain existing municipalities?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to page 15 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Just one moment, please. [Interpretation] The pages are numbered differently in my copy, so I find it difficult to follow, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I regret that I have to intervene. On page 49, in line 9, the witness mentioned some sort of agreement between Presidents Tudjman and Izetbegovic in Split. However, in the English, it says "they even signed some sort of split agreement." It turns out that they signed some sort of agreement on division. The word "split" has to be capitalised. It's the name of a town. This is the Split agreement, the one made in the town of Split, not an agreement about division. Could the witness confirm that? But we all know this. We have a document about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are talking about the town. We're not talking about division. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There's no disagreement about that. Mr. Kovacic is correct, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I could direct -- I'll do the best I can to assist you. It should be approximately at page 15 of your document. If you will find this section again where you begin speaking, after the president says -- The president says: "No, it is about partition." And Stjepan Kljuic says: "No, no. Those sons-of-bitches won't commit, they will not come out and say, 'Let us divide it, and you get this, we get that.'" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Further on in that same paragraph you say -- you're referring to people like Seselj. You say: "They're willing to give exactly the same thing, Western Herzegovina, minus Stolac and Mostar, you understand, with the Neretva as the border. The rest is theirs. They keep trying to accomplish this over and over again." Now, you've made several references in your testimony so far to meetings and conversations that you had with representatives of the Serbs or the Bosnian Serbs. Is what you say here consistent with what you've told us in your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing on in that same passage a couple, several lines down, you say: "In my assessment we would accept cantonisation if one of the cantons comprised Livno, half of Kupres, Bugojno, Travnik, Gornji Vakuf. These are areas where we have an absolute majority. But when it comes down to geographic maps, they will not accept it because there must be a logic to cantons and communications or geophysical position and so on and so forth." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had that proposal ever been made to the Serbs that the Croats would accept a division, a partition of Bosnia along the lines as you set out here?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two processes here. Earlier we spoke about cantonisation. That was a legal proceeding, and it had commissions of all three peoples. Those commissions worked, but unsuccessfully, because when faced with arguments, no agreement could be reached, and it explains here why; because the Serbs wanted territories even in areas where they amounted to only 5 per cent of the population. So one can see from this that they never seriously wanted there to be a new administrative structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina created through cantonisation but, rather, used proposals for cantonisation to express their territorial ambitions. Later developments would show that aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina was, first of all, motivated by the struggle for territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's me see, sir, if I could restate my question and you could answer my question. Had that proposal ever been made to the Serbs that the Croats would accept a division, a partition of Bosnia along the lines as you've set out here?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had such information, but the Croatian Commission of Cantonisation proposed our ideas to the Serbs about the administrative division of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serbs never accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your assessment in the same statement -- passage I've referred you to, was it your position that Bugojno was a majority Croat municipality?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But there was a large percentage of Croats in Bugojno. There was no absolute majority of any one of the two most numerous people, either the Bosniak Muslims or the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any particular percentage in mind which you thought at that level -- that percentage level it would be okay for one ethnic group or another to assert its power over that particular area? If it was 5 per cent Croat, 10 per cent Croat, 30 per cent Croat? When do you decide that that's enough to call it Croat?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never thought in those terms. But if one thinks about it logically, where there is at least a relative majority, there the Croats would have the advantage in the executive branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving aside from your particular comments at this point, which we'll come back to, if you go to page 17 of the document, you will find that then the second speaker appears to be -- well, other than the president -- Mate Boban. And his statement begins with these words: "All of you know that recently there has been an alternative entity in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, a continuity of the policies of the Croatian Democratic Union and the Croatian people in general. Something new exists called the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Community of Posavina in the north of Bosnia." Sir, was in the nature of the meeting that after you had made your presentation on your views that Mr. Boban was then asked to state his views to all those in attendance?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but he did ask to take the floor, and he did say that. And it says that Herceg-Bosna is an alternative solution for the Croats. So neither he nor anyone else has the courage yet to challenge the legally elected leadership of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you remind us again what position a man named Ignac Kostroman had in the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the business secretary or the administrative secretary. He dealt with the finances and the economy of the leadership of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to page 19 of the document. Mr. Kostroman begins to speak, and what Mr. Kostroman does is apparently read from the minutes of a meeting on the 23rd of December, 1991. If you see that. Starting on page 20.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is described as a meeting of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in expanded session with members of the BH HDZ Presidency from the territory of Herceg-Bosna and deputies from the territory of Herceg-Bosna to the BH Assembly.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you attend this meeting on the 23rd of December, 1991? The one in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody invited me. And even had they done so, I wouldn't have gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Kostroman at this time reads out the minutes of those meetings to President Tudjman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To everyone present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In item 2 of those minutes did Mr. Kostroman report the results of that meeting being taking the historic decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which serves as a legal basis for the entry of these territories into the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in item 6, this refers again to the conflict with you, is that correct, sir? On page 20 -- excuse me, page 22 of the transcript, item 6 of the minutes of that meeting being read?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear that for the first time now they are putting forward before President Tudjman the absolute differences in the interpretation of the implementation of the policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you can go to the next page, page 23, item 8. Did you see and did you hear at this meeting that the legitimacy of your position or your office in the party had been rejected, completely rejected at the meeting on the 23rd of December in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My legitimacy could not have been rejected, but from the report of the -- on the meeting in Herceg-Bosna, there was a demand that I be stripped of all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On item 10 on page 24, it says, "The legitimacy of Alija Izetbegovic, president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to represent the Croatian people in public is hereby revoked." Can you explain to the Judges, please, any legal authority or basis that this Community of Herceg-Bosna had to revoke the legitimacy of the president of the state?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither did they have the right to revoke my legitimacy nor the legitimacy of President Izetbegovic. These were simply the ambitions of those people who thought that all the competencies and authorities and powers should be taken on by the community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may intervene. If he could continue on and read the reasons why, and then perhaps the witness could give us an explanation as to whether those reasons were legitimate at the time, that is that the Croatian people felt that Izetbegovic and those in Sarajevo were not protecting the rights of the Croatian people in Bosnia as they were being attacked by the JNA and the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, again, Mr. Karnavas will have all the opportunity he has to conduct -- will have to conduct cross-examination. Everyone in the courtroom has this document in front of them. Everyone can read exactly what it says. I would like to be able to conduct the questioning. Mr. Karnavas can conduct his cross-examination as he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Having said that, to try to avoid any problem, Mr. Kljuic, assuming these statements are true, assuming for the moment that they are true, these references to the Serbian army's activities, did that give the people of -- the leaders of this thing called Herceg-Bosna that had been self-declared, did that give them any legal basis to reject the legitimacy of Mr. Izetbegovic as the legal president of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic was not advocating the interests of the Croats at those conferences on the Yugoslav level because this was being done by President Tudjman. Secondly, Izetbegovic was the president of the Presidency. He was presiding over the Presidency, which had seven members. And he never actually made an anti-Croatian gesture. He did, to be sure, say the war in Croatia is not our war, and he did have various options for the solution of the Yugoslav crisis, such as the one where Slovenia and Croatia would be a little more separate from Yugoslavia, Macedonia would be a little closer, Serbia and Montenegro would be the basis, but at certain points Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was not particularly skilful. A large percentage of Bosnian and Herzegovinian Muslims participated in the defence of Croatia, and there are documents to show this. There are many Muslim Bosniaks today who are veterans with rights in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kljuic. You were asked about the legal basis, whether there was some legal ground to declare that the legitimacy of Alija Izetbegovic had ceased, and you are giving us political explanations for the background. They have their value, but it would be helpful to the Bench if you answered exactly the questions of the Prosecution the way they have been put. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no legal basis for Kostroman, Kordic, Boban, and the rest to say that Izetbegovic could not represent the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me, sir, while I find the other passages most directly involving you. As we -- as I turn to those, sir, can I direct your attention, please, to page 74 of the transcript and continuing on over to page 75. At this point Dario Kordic takes the floor and about the third passage in that section, it says the following: "For six months we have been sweating blood deliberating over the idea that you presented to us on 13 and 20 June." Now, we've already heard that there were these two important meetings on the 13th and 20th of June. Can you tell the Judges a bit more about the idea that President Tudjman presented to these assembled groups on 13th and 20th of June, the ones that Mr. Kordic said they've been sweating blood about.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended only the first meeting, but at all these meetings the idea was always present about the unification of all Croatian lands into one state. This was not unusual, because the majority of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina were burning with the desire to accede to Croatia. This was a century's long desire. But in spite of this it was not realistic. Young people with no political education or experience fall in love with such an idea and imagine that God has chosen them to carry it out. So that at all these meetings where serious matters were being discussed, the structure of the future Yugoslavia, setting up economic relations, because you should know that the tension in the former Yugoslavia paralysed the life and work, the export of large companies and so on and so forth, this gentleman perhaps remembered only one thing of all this, that it was the desire of all of us that Croatian lands be united. For him that may have been the most acceptable thing, but it was immature and unrealistic because the political conditions and the situation, the status of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina determined their survival there. The fact that some people wanted there to be no Bosnia and Herzegovina in order that their goals could be realised was not enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was that Tudjman's view or just your view?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman spoke within the bounds of what was permissible. First of all - and this is perhaps most important - he wanted an independent Republic of Croatia. And as for Bosnia - I mean Bosnia and Herzegovina - whatever would happen would happen. And it was, therefore, possible for individuals to speak out at such meetings, and you can some extremist views expressed here in spite of the views of some serious people such as the late Damjan Vlasic, who was the president of the HDZ in Mostar. And you will see when the minister of defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Jerko Doko, tells the president, "But they're lying when they say there are so many municipalities." You know the people in Zagreb didn't know us really well. They didn't know where Kupres was. They knew about Mostar and Livno and so on, but they didn't know anything about Dobretici, they didn't know anything about Zepce, and so on. And in this situation, just as you here don't have time, for objective reasons, to go into details in order to see the background in which all this was taking place, neither did they. They said, "Well, what does it matter? Thirty or 48, let's have as many as possible."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Please be kind enough to slow down. The interpreters cannot follow you. I just said that, sir, I would like you to be so kind as to slow down because the interpreters cannot follow you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I really was speaking very fast. In such a situation, people had neither the patience nor the will to give serious consideration to all this. This was a general idea while Yugoslavia is falling apart, let's unite. This was in the heart of every serious person. But the political reality determining our fate in Bosnia and Herzegovina was such as it was, and it was part of my political programme. Until this meeting, never, either in Zagreb or in Sarajevo, had anybody officially risen against this policy. You were able to see at one point when President Tudjman generously says, "Stjepan, you have a lot of merit. You've been very good so far, but things are changing now." You see, I was not ready for those changes as a person who whole-heartedly belonged to the party, the Croatian Democratic Union. For purposes of national unity, I was prepared to leave. And in the text you can see that I'm offering President Tudjman and all the rest my resignation, because a conflict arose here between the legalists and those who did not respect the legal system. I could have set the meeting alight with a fiery nationalistic speech. There was a man there who spoke about what had happened since King Tomislav of the 9th century, since the 10th century, that President Tudjman was one of the two greatest Croats. These are words that sound fine, and he probably had some advantages because of what he said, but I didn't want to make those kind of speeches. This was a very difficult meeting. There's a specific way in which I fled from Zagreb at the time, but this was the end of the legal conception of the HDZ. From the 27th of December, other people would take the stage, front-stage people who would be acting contrary to our political platform adopted at the convention in Mostar. I'm sorry that a regular convention was not held where they could have presented their new political option and probably they would have had a majority and a new president and have been given legitimacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can turn your attention, sir, to page 105 of the document. After all these other people have spoken, you again become involved in the meeting. Stjepan Kljuic: "Mr. President, please, let me tell you, I cannot leave this meeting just like that, you know what the two of us have been through in this year and a half, you know all that I have done and what I have not." The president: "Kljuic, let us not waste time. We think, not only I, the Croatian leadership in general thinks that since becoming the head of the HDZ, you have all in all done a good job. I shall tell you, though, I shall repeat what I just said, that lately you have become closer to Izetbegovic's policy regarding these negotiations which we wanted. I have written down somewhere the date when we discussed how talks should be held with both sides, and our aim, our aim from the beginning, from the proclamation we issued, if you want, was not to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina as it is today. Essentially, this is not in the interest of the Croatian policy, as Croatian policy would in this way be permanently frustrated by the demographic and territorial loss in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Therefore, we finally wanted, and it was no accident that in the preamble to the Croatian constitution we also mention the Banovina of Croatia." Now, didn't Mr. -- didn't President Tudjman make it very, very clear to you now what his ambitions and what the plan -- what the Croatian programme and plan was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you've already heard, he said that everything was fine up until that time but that something new had happened, and that's why he put the banovina in the programme. However, if you want me to explain what the banovina was, I'll be happy to do so, but I have to say that it was not possible to implement it in practice because of the unsettled political question in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's talk sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- about 1991, December of 1991. Why was it not possible at that time to implement -- if it was not in your view -- not possible to implement the banovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't possible because a banovina disrupts the tissue of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and because of the territories that the Croatian Banovina encompassed on the basis of the 1939 agreement in September and destroyed on the 6th of April, 1944, today were not territories and regions where the Croats were in the majority. And to conjoin areas of that kind to the Republic of Croatia was impossible because of the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, among the people who did not show respect for either facts or reality, the banovina was some sort of ideal and obsession.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who were those people? You say among the people who had this view. Can you name some of these people who had this view that the banovina was "some sort of ideal and obsession"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first one was President Tudjman. You can see that today from this document. And the others followed suit, followed the idea, because at the time anybody who supported President Tudjman more would be considered a better Croat. And I say this now, they would have better chances of succeeding personally, on personal level. I gave up any possibility of doing so that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before we go on to another passage where your speak again, can I direct your attention, please, further on in the same passage we were looking at a moment ago where the banovina is mentioned. President Tudjman goes on to say, as referring to the Serbs: "The Muslims can come with us to Croatia and that way we would have the Muslims against us, but if we told them that we were in favour of their having a statelet of their own in the remnants of Bosnia, then they would have to be content with that." And did you continue to -- did you indicate to President Tudjman after that that you thought that was not a realistic situation? And I draw your attention to --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. -- when you begin speaking again on page 107. You may want to look at that. Can you look at that passage, sir? Can you summarise to us then what further you said to President Tudjman after he indicated to you that the Muslims would have -- would have no choice but to accept their statelet in a remnant Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was undermining the Muslims, and it brought to the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- it only did damage to them. You know the efforts that were made for the Muslims not to join the Serb side. From these documents -- well, you weren't able to see the great efforts invested by Milosevic to draw in the Muslims and attract them, either through direct office to Mr. Izetbegovic or through meetings of intellectuals or again through trying to get them on board, those Muslim Bosniaks who were in the police force and the army. So the Muslims at that time had become a mature people, and they were very conscious of their self. And anybody who questioned their national identity was an enemy, according to them. I was a politician from Bosnia-Herzegovina who considered that as far as we were concerned, at a point in time when there was aggression on the part of the JNA and Milosevic and Karadzic and Martic and that it had reached full intensity, that it was very important to have your Muslims on board as political friends and at the same time they were the ones who were in jeopardy. So to strip them of their identity and their equal rights as we and the Serbs enjoyed and say they would have to be satisfied with some statelet, automatically gave rise to resistance on the part of the Muslims. This reverberated very badly, to say they had to. Nobody had to do anything, because Croatia wasn't a force and power that could dictate anyone anything. It was blocked. A third of its territory was blocked, whereas in Bosnia, in December, 1991, many parts of Croatia, many regions were under Serb occupation, and many people had already fled at that time, had to flee. So as serious people we did look at all the variants and alternatives, but that kind of conduct and to say that the Muslims would have to accept what they were offered, either to join us, be with us or not, was completely wrong politically, and this led to the tragedies that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, continuing on where you next speak again on page 107, you start out by saying, "Mr. President, with all due respect, let me explain things ..." And then you go on to say: "The idea of 13 June was mine. Mr. Vlasic developed it, Mr. Doko and I brought you the papers here, if you remember, Vice Vukojevic and Mr. Ramljak were present as well, there were quite a few of us. "Therefore, I am not against it, but we agreed to put it into action at a certain moment. In my judgement, it was not the right moment." Now, what was your idea on the 13th of June that you claim "was mine," and how was it that it was not the right moment to implement that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people -- leading person, personages leading people in a wartime situation had to have a number of alternatives or variants, and this latter alternative, the last one, was this: If somebody brings us to a fait accompli, for instance, and as nobody brought us to a fait accompli, then what they were simply asking for was that we come out with options, come up with options which would disrupt the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when we mentioned these 30 municipalities, then that is the result of the Commission for Cantonisation and its work, the one I told you about. So everybody proposed cantonisation according to historical, national, geophysical factors and components which would lead to a grouping of municipalities with a certain majority. And when it came to cantonisation, the question of human rights were always brought up. So minority nations which would remain within administrative entities in the cantons of another ethnic group or national group which would be in the majority would be protected according to European standards of human rights. So that was that particular variant. Of course I said if that ever happens, and that was the last resort, which never entered my head to say this on the 27th of December, two months before Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised internationally. Because at the same time while they were going about their business, I strove with other Presidency members and the representatives the European Union and America that Bosnia-Herzegovina be given the same status as Slovenia and Croatia. And since everything had already been done to recognise Slovenia and Croatia, we were the next in line, and we succeeded in this. And I have to say that on the 22nd of May, 1992, we managed to have all three republics become members of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing on, on to page 108 after you spoke about what you've just described and again about the 30 municipalities, President Tudjman then responds to you: "Wait a minute. When we say that, you see 30 per cent of the Croatian territory, but what does this territory mean for the Croatian state? Therefore, if you consider only one element, it seems as if it should be rejected immediately. But you have to consider it in respect of what I said, that the State of Croatia cannot survive such as it is, but a Croatian state even within the borders of the banovina could, not to mention if these borders were improved on." And then you go on to say, "But, Mr. President, this version means that Knin and Drvar will join forces." Now, what did you mean by that, that his version would mean that Knin and Drvar would join forces?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the version that spoke of the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The president of the Republic of Croatia is calling for a banovina, and if he gets a banovina, then the Serbs will get their part and Serbian Drvar will link up with the Serbian Knin Krajina in the Republic of Croatia. And otherwise, the Serbs, all the Serbs, regardless of whether they were democrats or Chetniks, called for no borders between Serb lands. And I have to say that Martic, as the leader of Knin, with his police came to Drvar. So if President Tudjman gets his banovina, then the Serbs will link up Drvar and Knin and put a nail in the coffin of the Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, did you then go on to explain to President Tudjman that if some solution was proposed based on demographic majorities, that this would leave many areas outside the Croatian territory? I direct your attention to later on page 108: "Mr. President, in that case towns in which Croats today do not form the majority but which have a tradition that belong to the Croatian corpus, towns like Konjic, Mostar, Stolac, Derventa, Doboj, Jajce, Bugojno and Travnik would remain outside the Croatian domain." And did Mr. -- did President Tudjman have any response to that concern, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman, first of all, didn't like people answering him back, and probably I was the first person during the history of his rule, somebody who had more dialogue with him than anything else. You can see that on the basis of the documents. When somebody has a fictitious idea and when he poses that as a primary political task without taking into consideration any of the elements involved, then it's absurd to speak about whether those people -- or to tell those people that that's not a good idea. First of all, the banovina was not feasible. It didn't even take root in 1939. It existed for 18 months. It didn't have its army, it didn't have its currency or anything else, its administration, and so on and so forth. It never actually was implemented. And secondly, on the basis of that kind of banovina, which just lasted a year and a half, as a compromise solution to -- as a compromise by the Belgrade court to create foundations for a banovina in 1991 and 1992 was completely unrealistic given the prevailing conditions. And finally, the problem of banovina and the problem of Herceg-Bosna was that a large portion of the Croatian populace was left outside those administrative units. And that is why, as far as I'm concerned, as president of the Croatian Democratic Union and member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the only way out was an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, because if we had that, then we would be able to protect all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the Croats within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the passage -- continuing in the same passage that began -- the one I referred you to a moment ago, continuing on over to page 110 -- actually, if we can go back to page 109, excuse me. If we can find this, please: "The question is, how possible is it for us to achieve what the Serbs did in the Krajina and in Trebinje. I would like to congratulate these gentlemen. I would even be proud of them, and it even says in one of the texts submitted to you that the application of Croatian laws is demanded, that the application of Croatian laws is demanded in Busovaca, Travnik, Vitez, et cetera. "Gentlemen, municipal presidents come to me saying it is impossible to implement. I wish they could. "Furthermore, we consider that we should talk, but in all those talks, gentlemen, everyone asks who will be the first to propose a partition of Bosnia? Everyone one says let us see about cantonisation and so forth. When we brought the Serbs to the point of telling them you are the instigators, you will not be a part of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, and so on, please produce a paper on it, they only brought us a paper with a Belgrade initiative, but they have the press. "The question is, who will be the first to bite?" Can you tell the Judges, please, what this is all about, this question of who is the first to bite, and how did that enter into your discussions with President Tudjman and the other members of the leadership?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two points here. The first is that the people saying that a banovina should be set up and take over areas where they're not the majority population already on the 27th of December asked for the application of Croatian law in those territories. That is a paradox that just cannot be understood. The second point is this: When we set up the Commissions for Cantonisation, we prevailed upon the Serbs through argument to realise that if Bosnia-Herzegovina were to be divided, they would only have 31 per cent. And apart from that, that didn't satisfy their ambitions, because all over Eastern Bosnia - Zvornik, Visegrad, Foca especially - the Muslims were in the majority, and they wanted to take those areas. And later on, they did so militarily, and in Dayton they were given it in the form of Republika Srpska. So those political amateurs just kept talking and talking, "We're going to introduce Croatian law in Travnik, Vitez, and so on, they'll have to listen to us." I said that's not realistic. And when it came to a question of division, we could have accepted division only on the basis of cantonisation and the projects that were designed in an expert, scientific manner, not based on political pretensions or winning over territory militarily. We couldn't do that. The Serbs had already taken control of the areas they wanted to retain, and on the other hand I have to tell you that as far as I was concerned the most difficult problem was that any kind of division would mean that a large number of Croats would be left outside that community, and they were Croats in the large towns, and you must be aware of the fact that we had the largest number of literate and well-educated people, looking at the overall population census, and that in Sarajevo there were just 7 or 8 per cent of us because it's a large city, but culturally speaking, the cultural and public life of the city, there were between 30 and 40 per cent of us; university professors, actors, what have you, singers, et cetera, sportsmen and the like. So the Croats had the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question, and that is, please, I asked you, the language here says, "Who will be the first to bite?" Can you tell the Judges how that was a factor, a topic of discussion in this group, both on previous occasions and on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I think we're having a problem with the interpretation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Answer the question, please, again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As I was saying, when we started with cantonisation, we gave expert -- provided expert maps, and the Serbs saw that what they would gain in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not satisfy their ambitions. On the other hand, it was very difficult to assess the behaviour and conduct of certain individuals, regardless of their academic titles. Karadzic, for instance. He's a physician. However -- well, they were people that were just not suited to the posts they occupied. And they always asked for the maximum they could get. And what was most important is that the final borders and boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1699, territories changed rulers very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, we're not going to go back to 1699 now, but was it ever discussed in this meeting or in any other meeting that it was to the advantage of the Croatian programme if the Serbs were seen as the ones that had caused, that had instigated the break-up?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs already on a domestic level and internationally were seen as those who were destroying Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, I belonged to the circle of people who fought for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was very likely. Of course, the people taking part in the Zagreb meeting, among them there were people who couldn't wait for Bosnia-Herzegovina to be divided, either because they were in regions which would certainly come to belong to the Croats, or had some political ambitions of their own. But the fact remains that I did not allow, at least not in my name and through my presence, us to discuss that division. And I have to say that there were private contacts, contacts on a private level, because the Serbs were never idle. The Serbs constantly sought to find individuals through mediators, go-betweens, and so on, but you have to know that people were -- had kinship relations, family ties between the ethnic groups. But anyway, the Serbs tried to do two things, to inveigle the Croats to embrace the programme for Bosnia-Herzegovina and to compromise myself as being a Muslim man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention on to page 111 where you speak -- well, President Tudjman says, "Stjepan, let us be concrete now. Let us not waste time, please." Stjepan Kljuic: "The third version -- just let me finish, Mr. President, just two minutes. "The third version was that the Muslims would not want to come with us, that the Serbs wanted their part, so we would launch into propaganda about how this was a question of Europe and the Balkans, of Belgrade and Zagreb. Then we would have a chance of getting the Travnik Muslims, the Bugojno Muslims, those from Jajce, so Croatia would get a block. This should be prepared. "That is why we said we should have a commission for cantonisation."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. You see, when President Tudjman said that the Muslims don't want to, then the Croats would remain in Serboslavia, which would mean an expanded Serbia and Montenegro. We did not want to agree to that. And that was the only variant where I happened to agree with everybody in the hall. The whole thing we should not do is to stay in Yugoslavia. Now, it's a technical matter how we're going to step down, or out. On the other hand, if this was done on a broader basis, and in actual fact that was the conflict between the Balkan and the European in Bosnia-Herzegovina, those two elements, if that propaganda was put through, we would have greater chance of winning over some people who thought differently and who had their sights set on the West. It's not said here but it was assumed that there would be a referendum on that. And you know that we actually did have a referendum later on for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Anyway, all those alternatives and variants, the only task - and that was my special task - was to see that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina should not in any single part should remain in Milosevic's Serboslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that these three options that we've now discussed a couple of times today, these were all the points that had been under discussion since the meeting on the 13th of June, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with different intensities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So when the previous documents that were being discussed, and we saw records of HDZ meetings talking about the Commission for Cantonisation, this was all carrying out the discussions that had been had with President Tudjman on the 13th of June, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it needn't mean that. The Commission for Cantonisation worked on the basis of the documents that it was provided with, taking into account history, geography, geophysics, and so on, communication and those elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, you say, "Inside Bosnia and Herzegovina we should re-draw several municipalities." Why was that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just take a moment to find that portion, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Immediately after the portion we were just looking at.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here it is here. Well, you see here, during the communist era, many Croat settlements were abolished as municipalities in order to join them on to other national entities that were in the majority. There was the municipality of Ravno, in Popovo Polje, in Eastern Herzegovina, for instance, which was Croatian traditionally, a Croatian municipality traditionally, but in 1967 it was abolished and joined to Trebinje. Now, in Trebinje already at that time you had an absolute Serb majority and very orthodox political leaders, with the Communist label but they were pronounced when it came to Serb interests, and so the municipality began to atrophy and the Croats began to move out. They moved out of Trebinje and so on. The other case or example is a large Croatian settlement of Dobretici, which is located between Skender Vakuf, Jajce and Travnik, those three crossroads, and it was a good idea to link it to Travnik because then the Croats were the majority, or to link them to Jajce where the Croats once again were the majority population. But you know what happened, the Communists joined Dobretici to Skender Vakuf where the Croats were a negligible number, and of course Dobretici atrophied. They didn't have the finances, the educational system, the health system. So I suggested to President Tudjman -- and I'm sure he didn't know of this, he wasn't aware of that -- that by restructuring those municipalities you could get certain regions, and this was in our interest, for Dobretici to be joined to Travnik or Jajce. They would have preferred Jajce because of communication reasons, medicine, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- because I think I can finish the questioning, at least the Prosecution's questioning, on this document before the break. The Judges may have questions about the document as well. But if I can direct your final attention for this document to page 113. And after several -- you begin speaking again, and after the first two paragraphs or portions, then you go on to say: "Well, let me tell you regarding the policy here. It is not possible for the seventh dwarf to get up and make a ruckus about it. I did everything you told me to do. We cannot go on. You want Herceg-Bosna? You want Boban? Well, you're welcome to them, gentlemen. I resign. I'm always ready to resign Mr. President." Did you mean that, sir, and did you resign sometime after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you that this is a very clear dialogue between me and them. I did not agree to that policy, and even before this when we spoke privately in the president's home - and this was not recorded - I said to him, "Mr. President, you cannot get me to do this. There's little Boban who can hardly wait to do it." I was ready to resign. Maybe I was wrong. If the majority of the Croatian leaders wanted something and Stjepan Kljuic doesn't want it, then it's quite normal and an honourable course for me to step down. And that's what I wanted to do, but they did not agree to it. But 37 days after that, the finale arrived and there was a total split.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, so just so the record is clear, on line 22, page 75, when you said you had had another conversation and you said, "Mr. President," were you referring to President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions about this document, and it might be the appropriate time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So that the Bench knows where it's going, how much time do you need still?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To be honest, Your Honour, I hadn't thought about that in the last few minutes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I haven't really been thinking about that in the last few minutes, but -- give me one moment, please. Well, I would hope with a little luck we might be able to finish in an hour and a half. Maybe less. Maybe we can cut some additional items based on what the witness has already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Which means that the Defence will not quite have three hours. The Defence will have four hours tomorrow. We have three hours this afternoon, so it's going to be very short. For the time being, you have had five hours and 14 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Five hours or four hours? We have four hours and 45 minutes is what we have. Maybe there's some -- but in any event, Your Honour, I may -- I may have misheard. You said there were four hours tomorrow. Tomorrow is a full day, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm sorry. Yes, that's right. Tomorrow we have a hearing in the morning and in the afternoon. But that said, the Defence will have approximately the same time as you have had. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understood Mr. Scott, he indicated that I would have all the opportunity. That was his -- to quote him, all the opportunity to cross-examine. All the opportunity means that I should have the opportunity that is necessary for me to do the cross-examination, and as I indicated, given the complexities of what we're discussing and all the documents, that the time that I would need would be a lot more than what time the Prosecutor is spending, not to mention my colleagues, so I'm just saying right now I envisage the gentleman returning at some other point to The Hague because we won't be able to complete him by tomorrow. At least, that's what my opinion is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but I'd like to know this on the Defence side: Mr. Karnavas, are you going to be doing the cross-examination on behalf of the other Defence counsel? You cannot be entitled to six hours and all the other Defence counsel six hours also, so I'd like to know how you've worked it out between you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I've indicated in the past it's not easy to work out things. For instance, there's a new counsel in the case. I haven't met her. I haven't talked to her. I don't know if she knows anything about the case, so I don't know how I can divide any topics with her. But as I've indicated in the past, I represent a client and I have to do whatever I can for my client. Everybody else, if they want six hours apiece, they can have them as far as I'm concerned. Of course, I'm not the president of the Trial Chamber or the Trial Chamber, but we are we're all fighting for our time. I know that the Stojic team has a significant amount of questioning. I was told - I was told - that the Praljak team would give their time to me, or at least the majority of it, so they've been very generous. I don't know what the others are about to do. And I don't want to be in a position, Mr. President, that I'm pressuring others to give up their time in representing their clients and their clients' interests in order for me to represent my client. It just puts them in an uncomfortable position and in an unethical position. So with that being said, we will talk among ourselves over the break and we'll try to be as efficient as we can, but I can just see it right now, I see it that we're not going to be able to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but try to be efficient, because up until now this witness has only talked about political affairs and his meetings with Tudjman. He has never mentioned the names of any of the accused, so we are addressing questions which are of a very general nature. So we could expect to have a global cross-examination in response. This is how I'm trying to make things more rational, to avoid people asking the same questions, because after a few hours, I think we all understand what is at stake. Over the lunch break, maybe you could decide amongst yourselves what you can do. I don't know what the other Judges feel, but I don't think it is necessary to spend many more hours about what has already been said. So we shall take stock of the situation later on today. It is now 12.30. We shall resume after the break and resume at 2.00. See you then. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is now resumed. Has Defence been able to agree on the time they need to spend on their cross-examination jointly? Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I did manage to speak with one of my colleagues from the Stojic team, and it's my understanding that they need two hours. We will need -- we believe we need about six hours for the gentleman. I know that Mr. Praljak would like between 15 minutes to a half an hour, and I believe two member -- the other members wish to see how the -- will make a decision at the conclusion of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I will give you the floor. Personally I read the Kordic judgement on all those issues that we've been concerned about since yesterday. In paragraph 139 of the judgement, it can be summed up in six sentences. They spent hours on it also. So we are all able to do our sums and bear in mind judicial economy, but this has to be useful. So you have been -- you've just asked to have ten hours to cross-examine this witness on issues which perhaps the Judges will sum up in 10 to 15 sentences in the judgement. So that's in essence what it is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, with the utmost respect - with the utmost respect - the gentleman here is not just testifying about some minor issues. It goes to the core of the Prosecution's mode of liability, the joint criminal enterprise, and there are a lot of documents that might be useful in getting the gentleman's point of view, because perhaps they may shed light in a different light -- in a different manner, because it's our contention that what the gentleman is claiming today is not exactly quite accurate, and so that's why we need the time. We have a lot of documents. I keep repeating myself, but when the Prosecution introduces a lot of documents, knowing that the Trial Chamber is going to look at every single word, it behooves us, when we have the gentleman here -- and these are documents that the gentleman -- most of them the gentleman generated himself, or at least signed on behalf of -- as president of the HDZ. So that's the dilemma that we have. Now, the Prosecution, if they wish to tender fewer documents and narrow the scope of the indictment, then we won't need this much time, but the joint criminal enterprise is -- is an important mode of liability that cuts across on everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall see. If the cross-examination is not completed tomorrow, we shall have to see what happens at a later stage. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Two things very quickly. We have handed out just before we started - and I hope it's been provided to you already; if not, the registry probably has them - Exhibit -- it's in e-court, but it's Exhibit P 00081 in hard copy, which is the version of the minutes of the declaration on the founding of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, certainly the one that I had intended to use, and I provided that to all the Defence and to the Chamber, and again I apologise for the earlier confusion. I simply note that for your attention. Secondly -- secondly, Your Honour, I will say that over the lunch break I did go through and shorten my remaining outline considerably based on having reviewed the testimony and what's been covered so far, and I must say at this point I think the speed with which we're able to finish the direct examination will be largely dependent upon whether we can get concise answers from the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You are quite right, in fact, Mr. Scott. When the witness responds, it takes a long time. Witness, please try and answer in the most succinct manner possible. Sometimes a question is put to you and it takes you four to five minutes to answer that question. In a ideal world that's fine, but unfortunately, as I'm sure you've understood, we are pressed for time and we need to go to the essential, so please make an effort and shorten your answers, please. We would be most grateful. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I speak very short?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Be brief, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I wish to let you know that my business obligations are such that I cannot remain in The Hague after tomorrow. The president I work for is leaving on Monday on an international visit, and I have a lot of obligations in this connection. Secondly, at the Kordic trial, I was the expert confirming the authenticity of certain documents tendered to the Court, and I knew nothing about the possible crimes that the accused may have committed because I was in Sarajevo and he was in another area. The same applies to the accused present here. As I have already told the representatives of the Tribunal, I'm not aware of any crime that they may have committed and that I was in contact with them at the time. When I was the president of the HDZ, either they were not there or they were in minor positions. When they became the leaders, I had long left the HDZ, and also we were separated territorially. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for having clarified this. Rest assured you won't be asked to stay on until Thursday or Friday. Quite clearly, if you need to come back here, you will come back at a later stage. So as far as that is concerned, you need not be concerned. We have noted what you have said in light of what -- in light of the Kordic judgement and of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, if I could ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 00110 very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance to be able -- so you can see a bit more of that document, if you can look at that and confirm to us, please, is this a record of the decisions taken at a meeting of the Presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 16th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this is a meeting that you -- that you did chair of that body after -- well, on this date in January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph number 8, the efforts -- it says, "The municipalities close to the town to --" excuse me -- "to the town of Sarajevo that are not included in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna must immediately form the Sarajevo Croatian Community." And can you tell us, sir, whether that community was ever in fact formed in such a way similar to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or the Croatian Community of Posavina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither was there any intention to form the community on such a basis nor was it possible. It was formally established in the following manner: The representatives of the HDZ parties of those municipalities got together at a meeting, but it never took root, not even at the party level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, now I want to turn our attention to the next few minutes to the referendum that was held in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 29th of February and the 1st of March of 1992, on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Just by way of introduction, sir, can you confirm that it was the requirement of the European Community, as expressed through the Badinter Commission, that a referendum be held in Bosnia and Herzegovina to determine the wishes of the people in terms of independence from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Badinter Commission gave State status to Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as to the other republics, but in order for independence to be recognised, a referendum had to be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to Exhibit P 00116. And again I'll ask you to have a chance -- I'll give you a chance to see that. And is this the -- a record of the meeting of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna expanded to include presidents of municipal boards of the HDZ of BiH, dated the 29th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did you understand around this time, sir, that there were various issues or questions that developed among the Croatian Community, or at least the HDZ party and the Herceg-Bosna entity, about the -- what the position, what the Croatian position should be on the referendum and questions about the language used in the referendum question itself?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was more than one opinion, but the issue of the referendum or, rather, the question to be put at the referendum was formulated at the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina attended by the majority of Croatian deputies. I think 41 out of 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to understand that at least some part of the HDZ membership and the leadership of Herceg-Bosna found the existing language of the referendum question to be -- to present a problem, in terms of the sovereignty, what they perceived to be the sovereignty of the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but that was their personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reference to -- on the document, if you go to the heading, if you can find under "Decisions" overall heading number 1, but then it's the section that it states: "The historical sovereignty of the Croatian population of BH ..." And in the second paragraph of that section, it says: "Should the referendum 'for a sovereign BH' pass, the Croatian and Serbian nations will become ethnic minorities." And can you briefly describe to the Judges, if you know, in what way would the referendum as it was previous -- as it was then worded was it perceived would take away the sovereignty of the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's simply not true. First of all, it's a paradox that this community should be advocating the interests of the Serbian people; and secondly, the ethnic make-up in Bosnia-Herzegovina in that year was 44.3 per cent Muslims, 31 per cent Serbs, 17.4 per cent Croats, and the rest were either Yugoslavs or others. With the granting of independence, we would not have lost any of our sovereignty, because according to the then valid constitution, it said that Bosnia-Herzegovina was the state of its constituent peoples, Serbs, Croats, Muslims, in whatever order, and the other nations and nationalities and citizens living in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Skipping one paragraph of the document and going down to the paragraph that says: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is in favour of a referendum of BH citizens after certain acceptable conditions have been fulfilled." Did you have any understanding of what these acceptable conditions were?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't clear to me then, and it isn't clear to me now. The referendum was announced by the Assembly which appointed a commission for the referendum, and this was all within the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Any demands outside that were illegitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Before we leave this document to go back up to the first paragraph under heading one, the decision on the calling of the plebiscite. There's a discussion in this paragraph about a decision on the conduct of a plebiscite of the Croatian people in BH, that is in Croatian communities, to be held before the referendum. And just so there's no confusion between this plebiscite and the referendum that we're talking about, can you just confirm to the Judges that these were two separate -- two separate matters?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, you should know that before this the Serbs had called their own so-called plebiscite at which there were 22 per cent more votes than there were Serbs, and they said they didn't want any kind of independent Bosnia-Herzegovina but wanted to remain within Yugoslavia. As far as the international community was concerned, this referendum was not valid. We Croats doing whatever the Serbs had done to a lesser effect was simply not possible. The referendum in Bosnia and Herzegovina was called for the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1993. That was a year in which February had 29 days. In the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had to fulfil concern conditions with respect to the terms of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you there, first of all: You just said 1st of March, 1993. Did you mean to say 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2, 2. I did say 2. I don't know how it was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you please just indicate then, although this separate plebiscite was mentioned, can you confirm to the Judges that in fact other than the referendum itself held later in February, there was no separate plebiscite of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving on, sir, to -- directing your attention to the 2nd of February, 1992, at a meeting in Siroki Brijeg. Can you briefly tell the Judges how that meeting came about and what happened at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that meeting was called by people from Zagreb, the HDZ of the Republic of Croatia, and they informed me, as they did everybody else, that on the 2nd of February in Siroki Brijeg there would be a meeting of the Main Board and all the officials of the HDZ. Of course, that was an act of coercion, because I was still the legal president, and that meeting could have only been convened by the Presidency team of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But since it was supposed to discuss key issues of support or opposition to the referendum, despite this demeaning position, I did go down there. And a delegation of the HDZ arrived from Croatia, which included Stjepan Mesic, Vice Vukojevic, and Perica Juric, all three men highly placed within the HDZ of Croatia. I chaired the meeting, presided over it, and with me was Mate Boban, and for the most part all the representatives of the HDZ from all over Bosnia-Herzegovina were present despite the fact that the situation on the ground was very difficult at the time. The roads were blocked; you couldn't move along them. But I assume that everybody felt responsibility, and so they came to the meeting somehow. First of all, the first item on the agenda was the political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and of course many people asked to take the floor, and each of them presented their own vision of the development of the situation. However, I have to say that most people were quite reasonable, and that in the morning session, while everybody was rallied together there, they lent their support to me. It was an absolute majority support. However, then certain speakers began to take the floor who did not deal with the political situation but who were personally -- who personally spoke against me. At the time, I represented a great danger, you know, because I was the president of the Presidency as a legitimate body, and the situation became more complicated, and later on we were to learn that the delegation from Zagreb had an assignment to replace me. However, one of their members, he was to say this later on, when he saw the support I enjoyed of delegates from the ground, that they gave up on that idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you refer to this individual that you spoke with, was that Stipe Mesic, the current president of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did Mr. Mesic confirm to you that in fact he had been sent to Siroki Brijeg with the mandate to essentially remove you from office?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Siroki Brijeg but referral years later at a time when he became in -- went into opposition of that policy, he said, "You know, they sent me there to remove you, to replace you, but when I saw the support you enjoyed, we weren't able to do that."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you at that meeting ultimately indicate your resignation from the position of party president?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you just tell us briefly, then, at what point in the meeting did that occur, and what did you say in regard to your resignation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that the meeting was very laborious. It lasted a long time, and it was difficult, and some people from northern Bosnia-Herzegovina left the meeting. They said, "Mr. President, I'm with you, but I have to go to Bosanski, Gradiska, Samac, Bihac, or wherever, Brcko, and I want to get there before nightfall." You must realise that that was the 2nd of February, it was winter, the days were very short. And some strange people started entering the hall. They didn't have any legitimacy. And as the number of legal representatives was reduced and the number of these unknown people increased, the discussion took on evermore aggressive overtones. And they started saying, "Well, we're not going to be under the Turks because of Stjepan Kljuic. We want to go to Croatia." And one of the delegates - unfortunately he's dead now, he was a doctor - but he said it was all our people's dream to be in Croatia. Otherwise, he lived in the outskirts, the western district -- the western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was a predominantly Croatian area. So people got up. They made a lot of noise. They hurled insults, and so on and so forth. And at one point when the meeting no longer followed a normal course and when personal insults were hurled at me in a completely impermissible manner, I got up and said, "Gentlemen, I'm tendering my resignation. You go your way, I'll go mine, and history will show which of us was right." Then some of my -- some people who were attached to me, like President Mesic, et cetera, they jumped up. I'm not somebody who changes standpoints easily, who changes my mind. I was lucky enough to have to go to Sarajevo urgently, and when I arrived home two hours later, I had some very difficult health problems, and later on I was to end up in the intensive care unit of the infectious diseases ward in Sarajevo. Now, why did I tender my resignation? Apart from the uncivilised behaviour and the provocations hurled at me, I knew that the statute that we had enabled me to carry on as the president for some time. It said the "outgoing president." That was the term used. So nobody could replace me until a convention was held, a party convention. And I thought, Well, I'm going to try and bring about a referendum, call a referendum, and if I win then quite normally those who were against the referendum should leave the party. If I lose the referendum, then I'll leave. However, what I didn't know was that upon my return to Sarajevo, I would have a life-threatening health crisis over a period of 11 days. And I must say that none of the people from Zagreb even called up the hospital to see how I was doing. At that time, a man who was otherwise quite friendly towards me and was friendly with Mr. Tudjman, his name was Alois Mock, he was the foreign minister of Austria, he did call up the hospital and said he was ready to send a plane if I needed to be treated in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, we're going to continue on the referendum, and you've indicated now you were hoping to continue to support the referendum process. In that regard, let me ask you to next look at Exhibit P 00117. This is a meeting of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina Central Board, a meeting in Livno on the 9th of February, 1992. If you have that, sir, and if I can direct you to look at what I think will be the second page of the document. Did you come to understand there was a discussion of alternative language for the referendum that was being discussed by certain parts of the HDZ at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I see page 2, please? This, you see, this other -- second question asked by the referendum was a step further in the destruction of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, and apart from that, this question was put forward to the referendum commission, all was done legally, however, they were not abreast of the situation and tabled the proposal outside the deadline that had been set, so that regardless of the contents of that proposal, the referendum commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina didn't take the proposal into account because it came in too late. It came in after the deadline had expired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. We can just take this document briefly, but can you confirm that on page 2 there are two formulas -- two formulations of the referendum question. The second one on the page, the one lower on the page - if the registry can scroll down a bit - is it the second of the two formulations that was the actual language that had been approved by the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the ballot?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then if we go back up the page, was the language at the upper part of the page, was that the alternative language that was endorsed as a result of this meeting in Livno?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And before we leave that document, then, if you go on over to another page, there is a section that says: "The resignation of Stjepan Kljuic." If you can find that.
