And do you see there it says: "Mate Boban, presiding, explained that the resignation of President Stjepan Kljuic would not be a topic of discussion, because there would be a special meeting on this subject." Now, would there in fact be --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would there in fact be not -- not -- I'll come to this in a few minutes, but would there be a later meeting at which your resignation was discussed or dealt with?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite obviously Boban knew the statute of the HDZ very well. However, that convention was never actually held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did you find around this time, sir, that among the Croat people in -- Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was then some confusion over what their position or what their vote should be on the referendum in February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit P 00118. Perhaps as an example of that. If you can look at that for a moment, please. And can you tell the Judges what was the -- what was the discussion at the time, or the controversy or the debate, about whether the Croatian people should support the referendum, or vote, or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, refusal to accept it without question, the referendum question that was adopted by the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which there was active participation from the Croatian representatives as well, and subsequently the emergence of the Livno issue led to confusion among the people. And this was a small organisation in Visoko. Obviously it didn't have any strong contacts, so they wrote a letter and asked what the position was, to have somebody finally explain to them how they should vote at the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I can next ask you to look at Exhibit 122, or P 00122. Can you tell us, sir, that around this time, as you were recovering from your illness, did you have occasion to write a letter to President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Since I survived and when I was able to write with my own hand, I sat down and wrote a letter to President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is Exhibit P 00122 a copy of that letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I've seen so far, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Anything that you -- when you have a chance to look further at the letter, anything that you want to comment on about the text of the letter, you can do so concisely, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you scroll up, please. I think the letter was written in a very reasonable tone, and at the end, in order to dispel any fears, we asked that the Croatian people as a constitutive people of republican government should have parity representation like all the other people. And this was the first time that we were asking this - and I asked for it in the Bosnian parliament - that a house of nations be introduced as a body which would have the right to veto any legal decisions if they jeopardise the vital interests of any one of the peoples. And that same body exists today in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges, did you receive any reply from Mr. Tudjman or anyone on his behalf to your letter?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could next ask you to go to, or to be shown, please, Exhibit P 09616, which in the bundle skips down several documents. 9616. When you have a chance to see that, sir, can you confirm that this is the record of a meeting of the Presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 27th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll down, please. I didn't attend that meeting, but I do remember the statement from it, and it was this confusion among the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina that led to the fact that the people who decided had to choose, and I must say at the time that I was all in favour of a referendum and that I had the absolute support of the Catholic church in that regard to lobby for it. And that kind of situation made it incumbent upon the HDZ Presidency to state - and that was on the 28th of February, the day of the referendum itself - that the referendum question and the decision on Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence would not preempt a constitutional solution to Bosnia-Herzegovina, which means that they gave up the Livno question, and this enabled -- and also there was a subsequent statement from President Tudjman saying that the Croats should go out to vote on the referendum en masse. And not only did they have the largest percentage for independence, but they went out to vote, and there were 99 per cent of the electorate went out to vote, which means that hundreds of thousands of people, Croats working abroad in Germany and Croatia, came to Bosnia-Herzegovina to vote in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just looking again at the date of the document, sir, dated the 27th of February of 1992, can you confirm that that was exactly the day before the first day of voting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the continuation of the session on the 28th of February in the morning at 8.30 hours. So we must assume that they had met on the 27th, weren't able to reach an agreement, and continued in the morning of the 28th at 8.30 and then put out a communique, a statement. That is the day before the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you may have just said this, sir, but can you confirm, was this then finally the expression or the official statement from the party as to what the position -- or what the Croatian people should do in connection with the referendum?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, again before leaving this document, in item number 3 there is again a reference to your circumstance. Excuse me. "Until the competent body of the HDZ resolves the official, legal, and political status of the president of the HDZ of BH, Stjepan Kljuic, his rights and obligations with regard to his authority as the outgoing President of the HDZ of BH are frozen and he has no right to appear in public in the name of the HDZ of BH."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see that was a step further. At the previous minutes it said that a convention would be held. Now they can see that that wasn't feasible, and they prevented me from representing the HDZ of BiH. At the time, I was the party symbol, and I really did take the floor without any pretensions of representing them, but I took part in the struggle to win over the referendum. And I think I succeeded in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kljuic, moving on then beyond the referendum, there was also, around this time, a continuation of the Cutileiro peace process, and can I direct your attention briefly to Exhibit P 00123. Can you tell the Judges, please, did your colleague Mr. Markesic write a letter to Stipe Mesic in Zagreb recommending that you be among the delegation to go to the next meeting, the next session of the Cutileiro peace process at the end of that February?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you can then -- if we can ask you to look at Exhibit 124. Is that a response from Mr. Mesic dated the 20th of February, 1992, indicating essentially that you would not be included in the delegation but the delegation would consist of Mr. Lasic, Mate Boban, and Mr. Stanic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was any other explanation ever given to you as to why you were excluded? You still held the position as president of the party, at least officially; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But the Secretary-General Markesic managed to have Miro Lasic head the party rather than Mate Boban. This was quite a feat. And this led to their conflict in Lisbon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Conflict between who, sorry?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lasic and Boban, because Lasic was a minor personage in that party, and then suddenly he was appointed by Mr. Mesic as head of delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever play any role in any of the Cutileiro meetings?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before leaving this document, sir, can you explain -- give any insight to the Judges as to why did Zagreb have any role in any event in saying what the delegation should be? This is the party of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that couldn't have happened to me, to have somebody decide in Zagreb, even if his name was Stipe Mesic. But the people who took over the party after me, to them that was quite normal. And it's interesting to note that that particular conflict, whether to listen to Zagreb blindly and or to be independent, that is present, that kind of dilemma, in the HDZ to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can next ask you to look at Exhibit 187, P 00187. Just two questions about the Graz, so-called Graz Agreement on the 7th of May, 1992. Did you come to know around that time from press reports or what have you that there had allegedly been an agreement between Karadzic and Boban, dividing up a territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that agreement. The information that was given out was very meager. Before that, there was some other information to the effect that it was Mr. Manolic who had spoken to Karadzic, but there was already fierce aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina and our communications were cut off, and a lot of news items were launched tendentiously from all sides. So I don't know whether they actually met or not, or at least I didn't know until later on, through the Tribunal, I saw documents about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Before we leave the document, if you can just look at the text of the alleged agreement, and there is a Croatian language -- yes, there it is. Could you just look for a moment, please, at the items numbered 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may at this point just interject. If the gentleman is not aware of the agreement and doesn't know anything about it, now we're asking him to speculate on this document, and so I think that would be improper. Now, perhaps counsel could ask some non-leading questions and maybe through independent knowledge he may have an opinion or may have something to say, but I don't think it's proper for the gentleman to comment on a document which he has not seen and wasn't participated in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just state my question then perhaps it will be evident, and of course I will abide by the Chamber's decision in any event. My only question to the witness would be, if he looks at items 1 and 2, are the demarcations indicated there consistent with the various conversations and communications and meetings that he had been involved in with the Serbs over the past 18 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I withdraw my objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you've had a chance to look at items 1 and 2, can you simply tell us, based on what you've told us over the past day and a half, are these demarcations, not necessarily precisely, but consistent with the types of discussions, meetings, communications that had gone on between the Serb and Croat sides in the past year or so about dividing up Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's quite clear that after I left and stopped leading the HDZ, Karadzic did find partners for a dialogue. I have to say that among the majority of the Croatian people this gave rise to resignation, because at that time we were a victim of Milosevic and Karadzic. It's true that military operations had ended in Croatia, but there were new ones going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The village of Ravno was liquidated. The incident in Bijeljina had already taken place, and so on. So when aggression was perpetrated against the internationally recognised State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to negotiate with Karadzic was, first of all, immoral; and secondly, it was politically not viable. None of this was actually implemented. However, it was the policy of the new leadership of the HDZ to which I did not belong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, if I can just come back to my question before leaving this document. Can you tell us in looking at those paragraphs 1 and 2, again, you've talked this morning about various discussions, Western Herzegovina minus Stolac, Western Herzegovina plus parts of other territory, is that generally consistent with what -- the demarcations that we see in paragraph 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that in point 1 there's a misunderstanding. Karadzic is asking for the left bank of the river Neretva to be on the Serb side and all of the rest to remain Croat, probably, but the Muslims are not taken into account at all, and that's politically very irrational, not to use heavier expressions. And then the question of Banovina arises, because if Banovina is recognised, Karadzic doesn't have the left bank of the Neretva. These were misunderstandings. They might have reached an agreement elsewhere, but this was a key area. And this was never implemented. It was quite impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, finally, then, turning to your final departure from the party, was there a meeting in Bugojno on the 15th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. At that meeting, the HDZ suffered the greatest humiliation, the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was led by a man called Krpina. He was a dwarf from Zagreb, and I would have rather handed over the leadership of the HDZ to Mate Boban, because this was insufferable. But they called a meeting in Bugojno, and I didn't attend that meeting. My general secretary, Markesic, went, and there they appointed Professor Milenko Brkic acting president, and that put an end to my term as president of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak, you have just stood up. For what reason, please? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is the witness allowed to insult people, using words such as "dwarf," "third-rate player," and so on? I think the witness should be told to speak to people in a normal manner so that his testimony will make sense here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the French translation the word "dwarf" has been mentioned. You used the word "dwarf" because this man was very small or were you saying that this person wielded no political power? When you call someone a "dwarf," this can be insulting. So why did you use this particular word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It's not because of the objection. I will try to avoid saying things like this. He was not physically a dwarf, just politically. He was a low-level official, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that ended your time with the HDZ BiH; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. I think I was able to do a bit better than my estimate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Before giving the floor to Mr. Ibrisimovic, I have just one additional question I'd like to ask. Witness, you've been examined about your position as president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you explained at great lengths why you resigned at one point in time. What I would like to know is this: When you were heading this political party, what were your ties vis-a-vis the HDZ in Zagreb? Were you independent or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Politically I was independent. I created the political programme of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we had many standpoints in common, and I had support in Zagreb. Also, the interests of the Croatian people, both in Herzegovina -- Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia were identical. So it was not like a party in some state far away. It was all in a single country, Yugoslavia, but in two different republics. As for the political profile, I was certainly an independent personality, and they couldn't tell me, "Do this," or, "Do that." We Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina made a great contribution to the defence of the Republic of Croatia. We also provided humanitarian support. I was one of the first to organise a humanitarian aid convoy to Dubrovnik when it was under siege. We sent medicines and so on. So it was very difficult to separate the two, but politically when something had to be represented as in the interest of the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I remained absolutely autonomous for as long as I was able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have only a few questions for Mr. Kljuic, and I think I will give the rest of my time to my colleagues who may need more time and will make better and more rational use of it. I just don't know whether Mr. Scott wishes to tender his documents now or at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, very briefly, could you give us the exhibit numbers so that everybody knows what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was intending to do that at the end, but I'll try to do it now. I'm sure my case manager will correct me, I hope, if I'm wrong. Exhibit -- not necessarily in numerical order but I guess the order in which they were used. 0 -- P 09617, P 00015, P 0020 [sic], P 00032 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: One 0 missing in the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. 00031 -- sorry. That was -- 31 was admitted through Dr. Donia. 00020, then 00032, 00034, 00036, 00041, 00042, 00044, 00047, 00048, 00050, 00052, 00056, 00058, 00060, 00072, 00078, 00081, 00089, 00110, 00116, 00117, 00118, 00122, 09616, 00123, 00124, and I believe 187 has previously been admitted. I may have -- the registry can help me here. I may have omitted to say 09616, and that should be included. And I believe, Your Honour, I've been corrected. My staff has corrected me to say -- I think I said 00020. I am told that it should be 00022. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had noticed that. Registrar, kindly read out the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The following exhibits are therefore tendered and admitted with today's date: P 09617, P 00015, P 00022 and not 20, P 00032, P 00034, P 00036, P 00041, P 00042, P 00044, P 00047, P 00048, P 00050, P 00052, P 00056, P 00058, P 00060, P 00072, P 00078, P 00081, P 00089, P 00110, P 00116, P 00117, P 00118, P 00122, P 09616, P 00123, and P 00124. That should complete the list, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Ibrisimovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljuic, we come from the same part of the country. I've been following your work for the last 50 years, and your positions are quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphones please be switched on. The interpreters find it difficult to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the aggression --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There seem to be several microphones switched on in the courtroom. If they could be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Mr. Kljuic, we come from the same part of the country. As I was saying, I followed your political work, cultural, sports contributions in Sarajevo and Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout that time, for 50 years, and I know your position on the character of the war. In Bosnia-Herzegovina it is the JNA aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and you have a UN Security Council Resolution dated the 15th of May, 757, Resolution 757.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And your position is the same, that it is Yugoslavia 's aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On a sovereign country?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, on the Republic of Croatia and then on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and make pauses between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was first an aggression on the Republic of Croatia, then there was an aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That position was taken by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later on it was the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina when it brought the case to the International Court of Justice in The Hague against Yugoslavia because of what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm sure you're aware of that, know all about it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you supported that position, did you not? I don't know whether you were in the Presidency at the time.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not when that was passed, but I whole-heartedly supported it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I also know that the Republic of Croatia brought a lawsuit against Yugoslavia because of what was going on in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was to be expected as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to say is this: The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, later the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, never brought proceedings to bear against the Republic of Croatia before that same court of law.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they would, because we have to take into account all the events that took place and we would also have to take into account the arguments and the personal dialogues that Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic had, their discussions and conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your answer correctly, then it is your position that no such proceedings should have been initiated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Of course proceedings of that kind should not have been initiated in view of everything that the Republic of Croatia did for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who, during the aggression against [Realtime transcript read in error "upon"] that state were not able to flee to the east, they just fled to the west. And for a long time there were more than a half a million Bosnian-Herzegovinian citizens of different ethnic groups in the republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Through your testimony, and I know all this personally, that you, Mr. Kljuic, and I think Judge Antonetti noticed that as well, that they were one -- that you were one of the main protagonists of all these events, political events over the past 20 years in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What I want to say is this: While you worked as president of the HDZ, the two terms of office in the Presidency, you encountered many officials and representatives, high-level representatives of the international community, and also statesmen at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, or whatever other state, and many people at a local level that held certain functions. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to say is that throughout your work you were deeply involved with all the problems and the resolution of the problems that the Croats faced in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You were a very well-informed man, and you were a journalist by profession, were you not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning session, you mentioned this, I think, and from the aspects of my client's defence, not only did you never meet him, but you never heard of him either. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I heard of him, but I saw the gentleman the first time in court here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President. Ah, yes, I do. I apologise. Just one correction in the transcript. Page 106, line 8. It should read: "Aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Theoretically we should have a break in five minutes, but I think it would be better to have the break now, which means that the next Defence counsel can start on his or her cross-examination. We shall have a 20-minute break and resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First I just want to ask you a question with respect to something that was -- that you said in the Kordic case, and that is that prior to testifying in Kordic that you had been visited by some investigators, that they had taken notes, that you had made a statement, a written statement of which you signed. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of investigators. Whoever came to see me, I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe my question wasn't clear enough. Did you give a written statement, as you've indicated here - and I'm quoting from page 8735 in the Kordic case - you say, "There is a written record of what I signed as my official statement." Do you recall making that statement under oath in Kordic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, in the Kordic case you had indicated to the Defence lawyer that you would be happy -- you would be happy to fax the statement that you had signed as your official statement. Do you recall making a statement of that sort?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, but it was a long time ago. If I said that, if you have the document saying so, then I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you would be equally happy to provide me with a copy as well, would you not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got a statement to that effect among my documents, but if the court does, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I ask what happened to that statement that you provided apparently to the investigators, as you seem to indicate here?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You know why? In the Kordic trial, I was subpoenaed as well. I never said anything that the person in question did during the material time in the indictment. All I could have said is how he acted within the party on the basis of the documents presented today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But that wasn't my question, you know. Do you know what happened to the statement? It's either a "yes" or a "no" or "maybe."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I guess it's academic for me to try to ask it -- ask you to provide it to me since you don't know where it is.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave the statement, I signed it, but I don't have that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And may I ask, before coming here to The Hague, did you look at any documents, your previous statement, anything to refresh your memory in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Sarajevo and Zagreb, two books appeared, books of transcripts, and included there are the documents that I participated in. I looked through those, and one such book is in my hotel room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, and when you're talking about the transcripts, you're talking about the presidential transcripts, two volumes that are published and available to the public?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were published conversations between President Tudjman and other officials of the Republic of Croatia, and later on there were many others that I did not take part in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we get into the topics that I have, I want to pick up from where you left off --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to pick up where we left off with my colleague when he was asking you about Croatia, whether any -- where Croatia was taken to the International Court of Justice for any activities or any crimes it may have committed against Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you said no, and I believe you began talking about all the efforts, the humanitarian efforts that were made by -- by Croatia to assist Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it you know that Croatia was not only providing humanitarian aid but also absorbed a great many refugees during this period.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it also provided not just humanitarian aid but also it provided weapons to Muslim fighters; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, but I know very little about that. What I do know is that there was a general, Mato Sarlija, who quite openly helped and even trained Bosnian forces in the struggle against the Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know what period of time are we talking about, about what year?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be 1991, probably, and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, since we're on this topic we'll stick with it a little bit. We're talking about how Croatia is providing humanitarian aid and even military assistance to Bosnia-Herzegovina. In 1991, as we well know from some of the documents, Bosnia-Herzegovina was used as a staging ground by the JNA to attack the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, yesterday there was a document shown to you where the government -- the -- yeah, the state of -- or the republic of -- it would be a republic at that point, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is saying that it is neutral in this sort of conflict; right? They're staying out of it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that point in time, the republic of -- I guess it would be the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time, it was still part of whatever was left of Yugoslavia. Correct, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the Socialist Republic. We took that prefix away, but it was just the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So -- but nonetheless, Bosnia was declaring its neutrality while at the same time allowing its territory to be used by the JNA to attack another country; right? We'll talk about whether they could have done so --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you don't understand the situation that we were in, well, we were a country in which there were the largest number of soldiers in the world and where the Yugoslav People's Army ruled. The regular authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina was amputated in a large portion of its territory. The areas from which the Republic of Croatia was shot at was not under the control of the legal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me rephrase my question, and I apologise for being ignorant of the facts, but I understood that it was on territory within the geographical borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina that the JNA - and I believe you called them Chetnik forces - were attacking the Republic of Croatia. Now, that's either a "yes" or a "no" or "I don't know." Which of the three?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that that was so. But you must know and realise that within the territory of the Republic of Croatia there was also space and areas from which there was firing at the regular forces of the Republic of Croatia, and that was no precedent. The Serbs did the firing, the JNA did the firing, the Chetniks, Milosevic's forces, Martic's, Karadzic's forces on those free areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to be step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And first what I want to confirm from you is the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina says, "We're neutral," but at the same time, albeit they couldn't do much about it, they said to the JNA, "Izvolite." "Here, you can use the ground, attack the Republic of Croatia," and nothing was done by the government in Sarajevo of which I believe you were a member of, of the Presidency. I guess that's what I'm trying to do, set the ground. And we're going to talk about whether Bosnia and Herzegovina could do something about it. But the bottom line is that the JNA was using what -- territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina to attack Croatia. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, it's very difficult for me to talk to you because you don't seem to understand me, and you don't understand the situation either. When we say that Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed neutrality in the conflict between the Serb forces and the regular forces of the Republic of Croatia, that means that that was the most we could do in view of the political composition of the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And not -- and certainly not -- we did not give legitimacy to the JNA forces and the volunteer formations to fire at Croatia. Quite the contrary. We prevented the Croats and Muslims from joining and going to the JNA. You know that Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time still belonged to Yugoslavia and that to sidestep your military service or your -- or joining up the army was a very drastic violation. Hundreds of thousands of young lads of ours fled in the face of the Yugoslav army who wished to mobilise them. So not only did we prevent that from happening as far as we were able to do, but we did not have the means of preventing the shelling of Croatia from the territory and areas which had previously been occupied either by the SDS or the JNA or the volunteer units and organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to talk about what happened to the arms. We're going to talk about what happened to the TOs, the territorial -- we'll talk about that. But now when you're saying -- you gave us an explanation about this neutrality. Some might say, would they not, that Izetbegovic, who at that time said this is not our war, is on the fence, waiting to see who is going to win, and perhaps hoping or waiting or expecting the JNA to win, in which case he's aligned with them. That was one of the perceptions at the time, was it not, of what Alija Izetbegovic and perhaps those who were in his Presidency were doing? Perhaps present company excluded.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you have to separate the statement made by Alija Izetbegovic from the activity of the Presidency. Secondly, he did make that statement, and it had very negative repercussions. Not only among the Croatian people but also among a large number of Muslim Bosniaks. There was nothing he could have been waiting to see, because all of Bosnia and Herzegovina was an enormous barracks at the time. However, in spite of what he said, a large number of Muslim Bosniaks were of a different orientation and played an active role in the defence of Croatia. It was not possible to wait and see, because in 1991, we had achieved an agreement in principle with the army that it should respect the civilian authorities. However, you also are a gentleman from the Balkans, so you must know what people say on one day is not binding on anyone in the Balkans. Therefore, the Serbs, together with the JNA, continued shooting on Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and firing, but they were doing so illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's stick with this just a little bit, because we're getting away from my -- my outline for your cross, but when -- when Izetbegovic is saying this, this is not our war, when the JNA is being -- is using Bosnia-Herzegovina territory to launch attacks against Croatia, do you think that those actions might instil fear in the Croats that are living in Bosnia-Herzegovina that perhaps this particular government in Sarajevo is not necessarily looking after their best interests? Maybe they can't, but they certainly are not looking after their best interests.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the government in Sarajevo consisted of representatives of all three nations, including the Croats. Secondly, we were in charge of the defence department. A Croat was the minister of defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But everything was possible in peacetime. We were unable to stand up to the army because of a mistake made by the Communists of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1989 and 1990. I tried to explain yesterday how Josip Broz had two military formations. One was a professional armed force with its regular composition and young conscripts, whereas the other was the Territorial Defence. The Communists of Bosnia and Herzegovina, just like the ones in Croatia, agreed for the weapons of the Territorial Defence to be confiscated, thereby rendering impossible any kind of resistance to the aggressor. The Slovenes in whose national tradition there is very little of war did not give up their weapons, and they managed to defend themselves very quickly. So it's not true that this government which included Croats did nothing to oppose the Serb aggression. We asked for international protection, especially later on when Bosnia and Herzegovina was received into the United Nations together with Slovenia and Croatia. But there was very little objective power to stand up to the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to be cutting you off a little bit. I let you go on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I let you go on a little bit, but I'll be cutting you off a little bit so we can stay on schedule, because we'll here two weeks at this rate. I asked you about how the Croats might have felt in light of the inaction of the government in Sarajevo. You're telling me they were doing something. I suspect the folks in Ravno that were massacred, and their families, didn't feel that way, and especially didn't feel particularly welcome by the Izetbegovic crew when Izetbegovic stands up and says, "This is not our war." And I'm talking about perceptions. I'm not talking about the government could do. I'm talking about what people are perceiving, which might be a reason why some folks are beginning to think that maybe they should arm themselves.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. It's correct that Izetbegovic made more than one statement and that his behaviour at that point was perhaps not entirely correct, but what were we to do; quarrel with Izetbegovic? You should know what the context was and in what conditions the people were who were exposed to Serbian aggression. A third of Croatia had fallen and no one could say anything. In that are period, leaving aside what Izetbegovic said, the Muslim people felt solidarity with the Croats and wherever there were Croats living together with Muslims where the Muslims were in a majority, there were no problems at that stage. The problems arose only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday you were shown a document by the Prosecutor. I believe it was 00060, and that's the document where actually the word "neutrality" appeared. And if I could direct your attention to paragraph 5. It's on page 2, and I'll just read it. It's very short. It says here: "The decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the neutrality of Bosnia and Herzegovina is endorsed, but - but - with the condition that Bosnia-Herzegovina will not nor will it be a military training ground for continued aggression." Now, I take it, sir, that was perceived at the time -- or Bosnia-Herzegovina was perceived to be at the time a military training ground for continued aggression; right? That was what was perceived by the HDZ. And we're talking about October 8, 1991, signed by none other than you yourself as the president of the BH HDZ. So those were your sentiments at the time, were they not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we get into more documents, first I want to cover some of your background a little bit because I don't think we have a full background. We talked a little about your education. You indicated some time in Zagreb. I believe it was philosophy, literature. And then I believe you continued your education in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at some point you became a journalist by profession.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, that's a pretty wide profession. That's like saying a lawyer. You could be a lawyer of a variety of things, tax law, criminal law, whatever. Could you tell us, what exactly were you covering? What was your beat?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I was dealing in culture in Oslobodjenje in '64, so the arts. After that, very soon after my ambition to write about politics, I was moved to the sports page. Then I was dismissed from Oslobodjenje, and for a while I was unemployed. Then I got a job in the Zagreb paper Vjesnik, which is the most eminent newspaper printed in the Latin alphabet in the former Yugoslavia, and I became a political journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This lasted for a relatively short time, and then I was suspended. After a session of the Central Committee of the Communist Party in Karadjordjevo on the 21st of December, 1971. The entire party leadership of the League of Communists of Croatia was replaced but so was the leadership in the newspaper company Vjesnik. For a while I composed crossword puzzles, of course anonymously, and then I wrote about sport and the arts and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if -- so primarily you were a sports writer, dabbled a little bit in political writing, but of course during the period that was impermissible, which is why they shifted you around. And I take it when the war -- or when the system is changing and you're going into a new -- the free elections are coming up, that's where you're found. You're found with that sort of experience as a journalist; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before the democratic elections, I was rehabilitated. So in 1990 I was writing about politics again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you say "rehabilitated," you indicated yesterday you were a dissident. Could you please tell us how much -- were you ever put in prison for your political beliefs as a dissident?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, could you tell us, what kind of a dissident were you? You say political dissident, but I mean what -- given the -- the government at the time when you were "a dissident," as I understand it a couple of topics were taboo. One was politics. The other was anything that had to do with nationalism. So ...

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, not all those who were in prison were dissidents. There were various misfortunes. I was never even before a misdemeanour judge because I have obeyed the law all my life. I've always been law abiding. It's hard to explain what sort of dissident I was. I can try to explain as follows: In 1970 I was awarded Journalist of the Year award in the morning, and then when a high-ranking party official learned that the prize had been awarded to me, he abolished the prize. At 12.00 noon, the secretary of the Journalists' Association called me up and said Get dressed up. Well, I was always nicely dressed anyway, but he said get dressed up and you will be awarded a prize in the evening, and then at 4.00 p.m. he calls me up and says, Don't bother to come, your prize has been abolished. Then, for example, in professional promotion --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here for a second. This scenario could have been because you wrote a bad review on a sports event too. My point being that you kept saying yesterday that you were this well known dissident, dissident, dissident. We come to find out now that perhaps other than what you're telling us, we have no proof that you were indeed a dissident of some prominence in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not here to prove whether I was a dissident or not. I know what I was and I know how my career was denied. But you should know that in 1984, I was awarded the main journalistic prize in Bosnia-Herzegovina for writing about literature. I don't think my career as a journalist has anything to do with this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we're going to go step-by-step. 1990, you've been -- you've been cleared. Now you're back in politics, or you're writing about politics. Suffice it to say, when the HDZ is being formed, you have no practical experience to speak of in politics. That doesn't mean that you're not a charismatic politician capable of organising and perhaps designing a platform, but you have no practical experience to speak of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're wrong. I had an enormous amount of political experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that would be as a dissident?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. But I was never a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But now this -- and I don't want to spend too much time on this dissident issue, but was this a party of dissidents that you had organised, with cells and -- I'm just asking the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I would like to ask you be so kind to slow down a bit. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, if you write an article saying that in Sarajevo the main streets are called after Serb rebels and soldiers and the street named after the main Bosnian King Tvrtko is only a few hundred metres long --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I don't have time for these discourse. I'm just asking you a very basic question. Could you --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have even less, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Good. We're going to try to get you home tomorrow then. So my question is --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll certainly come -- go home the day after tomorrow. You know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course. Of course you will. But I was hoping that we would finish the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I can't keep anybody over here anyway, so don't worry about what I say.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not worried. I've never been worried in my life, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you belong --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please try to answer the question. You might not like the questions that are put to you, but the cross-examination is conducted in such a way that Defence counsel is entitled to ask you any question he or she likes. But please calm down, because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm a very stable personality. I'm not excited at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- let's move on. With the -- at some point political parties are allowed to be formed in the former Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what is the period again, just to refresh our memory? Starting what period?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the beginning of 1990, and there were some parties that were initiated towards the end of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct. Now -- and it's at that point in time when you begin to get involved formally, at least, in politics. Formally and openly as well.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started getting involved in politics formally and openly when the possibilities were opened for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you indicated to us that you were one of the founding members of HDZ.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, as I understand it, when -- when HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina was founded, the former Yugoslavia was still intact.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so that's why one could look at HDZ Croatia and look at the HDZ Bosnia and they would see that they would be associated. One may be the parent, the other one the child, or brother and sister, however you want to look at it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sisters, sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Sister. And so you saw yourself -- well, you were indeed the president of this -- of HDZ in Bosnia, while at the same time the late President Tudjman was the president of HDZ in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was president from the 16th of September, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to make sure that we understand, at least while you were president, during your tenure, you were not receiving orders from Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had meetings. What the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HDZ of Croatia had in common we talked about. As for representing the Croats in the official talks among the presidents of the republics, President Tudjman was looking after us because Mr. Izetbegovic was representing Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to stay with that a little bit, okay? You said, you know, whatever you had in common. "Common" was, I guess, the Croatian people and their interests; right? That's what the two parties had in common.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and a number of other elements; cooperation, gathering the diaspora, cultural cooperation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you say "gathering the diaspora," as I understand it, and maybe I'm wrong, a Croat in Cleveland, Ohio, is just as good a Croat as if he's in Zagreb or in Sarajevo or Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. But when we talk about the diaspora, you have to know that there were far more Croats in the diaspora who originated from Bosnia and Herzegovina than there were from any other part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But I guess the point I'm trying to drive at is that these were considered just as much Croats. They weren't considered, well, they're half Croats because they're in the diaspora. They were considered Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And this was a rather historic period for Croatia as well as for Bosnia-Herzegovina, but particularly for Croatia because for the first time now, at least in the last 50 years, they can have -- you know, they can be outside of the former Yugoslavia and within the borders of a Republic of Croatia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it as the war was looming, and then throughout the war, the Croats, both in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, relied heavily on the diaspora Croats for contributions, for assistance.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at some point, as I understand it, Croatia, the Republic of Croatia, allows Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina to also have passports and become citizens of -- of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had dual nationality, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And was that also provided to Muslims at the time? Not all, but --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes. Today there are still many Bosniak Muslims who hold Croatian passports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there's nothing unusual or nefarious about the fact that Croatia is allowing Croats in the diaspora or Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina to have dual citizenship?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's more than one European country - for example, Italy - that follows the same principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to talk a little bit about the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Not just them but also the other two nations that comprise members of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Where I come from, you would just be a citizen. You're a citizen of the United States, maybe a resident of Alaska. But in -- that's not the case in -- that wasn't the case, and it's still not the case in Bosnia where you had three different nations recognised within the constitution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It's a very important difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please, sir -- and I know you're not a jurist, by your own admission, and perhaps you're better off not being one, but could you please tell us, what is that difference as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you should know how the USA developed historically. They have only had a state for a little more than 200 years. Secondly, that state neutralised its indigenous people politically, and it became a state after immigrants arrived from various parts of the world. And you know that it wasn't clear until after the war what language would be official, and then a referendum was held and the English language --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... tell me about the three constituent nations of Bosnia. Why do you have nations as opposed to just Bosnians? It's like one word; Bosnians, it covers everybody that lives in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Make it easier. Why don't you have that? Instead you have, in the constitution, three constituent nations.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlike the USA, which established a nation in the way we have described, before nations were formed in the European sense there were religious communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Up to 1964 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note we did not hear the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, until the schism between the Catholic and Orthodox churches, there were Christians in Bosnia. Later they divided into the Orthodox and Catholics, and various other sects arrived and other movements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. I've interrupted because I would like you to speak more slowly, both of you, and you overlap, and the French and the English don't tally. So please speak more slowly. This may ease the tension.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, upon the Turkish occupation in 1064, or 1463, regardless of the religion that prevailed before, they were not only Orthodox and Catholic, there were other sects, they espoused Islam, and with the subsequent historical events, three groups were formed as communities on a religious basis. In the 16th century, when Filip IV expelled the Jews from Spain, you had Jews arriving into Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was the first time that four large monotheistic religions came into existence. With the development of the bourgeois classes in Europe, and in the Balkans that was little late, it lagged behind Europe, but the nations were formed. As the Serbs and Croats were the first to form their own nations and the Jews remained in the state they had been, then there was a group of people that were most numerous in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were of the Islamic faith. The political emergence of these religious communities into national or -- communities were -- occurred in '68 and legalised in the population census in '71.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So this brings us to date.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This brings us to date. Now, I take it -- you indicated to us the percentages. If I recall, it was something like 44 per cent were the Muslims that are today called Bosniaks --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 43.4 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. And then it was 31 -- or why don't you just tell me.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 43.6 per cent Muslims who are Bosniaks today. 31 per cent Serbs, 17.4 per cent Croats, and others who were either Yugoslavs, that was this post-war creation, or the members of other ethnic groups such as Montenegrins, Albanians, Slovenians, Hungarians, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And I take it for the Croats who were only 17.4, it was pretty important for them to make sure that they just didn't lose their -- their status as a nation; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And of course if you were to have a government, a democratic government where you would have, say, one person, one vote, everybody's equal, everybody gets one vote, one could say, at least in theory under that particular system, the Croats would be the losers, being 17.4. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't put it that way because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to build on it. We're going to build on it step-by-step. So first --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I can get my answer, and then we can move. We'll move on from there.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically speaking you can put it the way you've just said, but I have to make you aware of one particular fact that you don't seem to know about. It was agreed in the first government that capital decisions must be taken by consensus on the part of all those present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- but getting back to what I was saying, one person, one vote would not guarantee the -- the vital national interest of the Croatian people; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that had been a question that had been looming in the air among the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was a concern, was it not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the one-party system, there was no concern at all because the executive organs of power and authority were elected by the party cadres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're talking about back in the former Yugoslavia days.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Where you could be a Montenegrin and just have -- just -- you know, with 3 per cent of the population, and still --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Prime Minister in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Now -- but my question is this: Now you're moving into a different era. You're moving into a different era with Bosnia-Herzegovina wanting to declare itself independent; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We already know from what you told us that the Serb, they decided to have a plebiscite, and based on their wishes, they wanted to stay within Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Croats, if I could say -- if I could speak for them, under no circumstances wanted to be in -- wanted to be in --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, don't speak for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They didn't want to be in Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And -- and what about the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did they have a clear position from the very first day, or did it sort of fluctuate and eventually gravitate in one direction?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims did not have a clear position from the very first day. What they wanted was to remain in Yugoslavia, first and foremost. And that was because, among other things, because there were Muslims in other republics; Montenegro, Serbia, Macedonia. However, as events developed and as the aggression burgeoned and became ever more brutal, the Muslims ultimately opted for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was reflected in the referendum of the 29th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, that's the referendum where -- where there was that famous question that came into -- into question among the Croats. There were two factions; right? There was one faction that --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's putting it mildly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm glad I'm putting it mildly for your amusement, because at the time, I take it, there was a rather important event, particularly given that members of the HDZ thought that you were letting them down, that you were not supporting the appropriate question which would guarantee their vital national interests. That was their perception. Not mine, theirs.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not right on that score, because, before that, there was a great test for us Croats, and it was this: In the preparation for the democratic elections, the Serbs came out with a proposal according to which there should be three members of the Presidency who would be Muslims, two Presidency members would be Serbs, one Presidency member would be a Croat, and one would be the representative of the other citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here, because I'm not -- I'm not here to talk about what the Serbs were up to. We're here to discuss about what the Croats felt regarding the question that was ultimately put, and I put to you, sir -- perhaps you can correct me, but I put to you that there was a large faction in the HDZ which felt that you, you personally as president of the HDZ were not looking after the vital national interest of the Croat -- of the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina because you were backing the question, the referendum question that was preferred by Izetbegovic and company as opposed to the question that they were proposing which they felt was more appropriate to ensure that 17.4 per cent of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be protected, their vital national interests would be protected. Isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, none of what you said is correct. I have tried to explain to you how I represented Croatian interests when, during the communist regime, I entered the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Izetbegovic and Karadzic were there and the existing regime, the regime that be. And the proposal to elect 3, 2, 1, plus 1, I stood up and said we Croats would never accept that. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just take it slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, please allow me to finish. You know what? I'm an amateur here compared to the professional teams working here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Allow the witness to finish, because your question is a very interesting one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it require -- it brings to mind -- to the witness's mind developments. So let him reply. Your question was a long one, and it deserves having a comprehensive answer from the witness. So go ahead, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, when the proposal was made to have an asymmetric representation in the Presidency without parity, I was the person who blocked that. I didn't ask the base, I didn't refer to Zagreb either. And the fact that two Serbs, two Croats and two Bosniaks -- or, rather, Muslims, plus one other, that that was the schematic, was to defend Croatian constitutionality and equality in the top echelons of the government. The fact that you're saying I didn't take into account the vital interests of the Croatian people, that's something I'm hearing for the first time. I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps I can help you understand because I think really there is a misunderstanding now. Mr. Karnavas was not suggesting any such thing to you. He was only asking whether there was a part of the Croats who thought in that way. Maybe wrongly. But the question to you was were there some Croats who thought that you did not properly defend their interests, and that's the question you are invited to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, possibly there were such people, and you were able to see on the basis of the documents that they even made their views felt in party meetings, but the question asked at the referendum was not Izetbegovic's question. It was a question relating to the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina without any additional cantonisation. Additional cantonisation was the product of negotiations that were taking place behind my back by certain HDZ representatives with Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps it might help a little bit if we look at the two questions side by side. All right? And by the way, I'm just expressing what the perceived viewpoint was, not my personal viewpoint. I wasn't there, I couldn't vote, nor do I have a say in any of it. If we could look at I believe it's 00117. That was the Prosecution's document, and this was shown to you, sir, earlier. It would be on page 2. It's dated 9, February, 1992. And this is in regards to a meeting that took place in Livno that -- I understand, sir, you were not present in Livno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But nonetheless, you are familiar with that particular meeting that took place there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, you being the president of the HDZ at that time -- or were you? Were you still the president? I know you had resigned, but were you still receiving -- this is 9 February, 1992. Were you still the president of the HDZ at that -- at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the status of outgoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. With the status of outgoing, but nonetheless you -- and I take it that you had in fact at the time, you had seen the record from this particular meeting that took place on 9 February, 1992. It was the BH HDZ Central Board. You've had a chance to look at the minutes of the meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm saying not today but back then you had an opportunity to look them over. As president of the party, obviously you must have been curious to know what your colleagues thought and the discussion that took place concerning this very vital issue that affected not just the Croats but also the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I didn't see the detailed contents, but there was a news item with the following formulation, put that way. Now, you either happened to forget something when I spoke about the referendum questions, the referendum commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The question was adopted first at the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina where the Croatian ministers took part, and then subsequently in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which our representatives participated, which means that that formulation was a legal one and it was passed down the institutions of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The one that appears -- the formulation that appears in Livno --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I don't mean to cut you off, I certainly want you to give your full answers, but if you could just work with me a little bit, okay? I'm not questioning how -- my question doesn't go to how the first question was formulated or whether it was proper or improper. What I'm saying -- what I'm asking you is you as president of the HDZ at the time would have looked at the record and would have reviewed what your colleagues were saying with respect to the two options that were on the table. Option one, the one that was going to -- that was being proposed. Option two, the one that the Croats within the HDZ that were in a different faction than you were promoting at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, none of them belonged to me personally as Stjepan Kljuic. The first variant was a proposal by the government, adopted by the Assembly, where not a single Croatian representative voted against that formulation. It was adopted and then sent on to the referendum commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, again --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, in Livno --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to talk about what happened in Livno. What I want know, sir, is did you in fact review the record of the meeting that took place in Livno on 9 February, 1992? It's a yes or no answer. It could be, "I don't remember."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, because I didn't receive it. They didn't treat me as president any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So are you suggesting, sir, as of 9 February, 1992, you were not receiving any documents from the HDZ? Can I conclude that from your statement, from your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the 9th of February, I never again received a single document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it as you stand here today -- well, let's me -- let me just rephrase that. As you stand here today, did you have a chance to review the record at some other point, to at least see what the discussion was all about?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that formulation from Livno, known as the Livno question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you again.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- brought to light --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you looked at the record? I don't mean to be aggressive and I certainly don't mean to be disrespectful. I'm just asking you at some point in time, after the Livno meeting, have you looked at the record to see what your colleagues were saying, what the discussion was about? That's what I'm asking. It's a "yes," "no," "I don't remember." Three options. That's the universe of choices.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the records but I did see the formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
